Relational Algebra

Chapters 7 & 8 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 7.1–7.9, 8.1–8.5, 8.9–8.12, 8.15–8.22. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

Relational algebra is the formal query language under SQL. Each operator takes relations and returns a relation, so operators compose into query trees. Every query here is evaluated on the COMPANY state of Figure 5.6, so you can check each result. Build queries from named intermediate relations, and project to compatible attributes before any union, difference or division.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  Overview: what relational algebra is

    Theory recap

    The relational algebra (RA) is the basic set of operations of the formal relational model. Every operation takes one or two relations and returns a new relation, so operations can be nested (the algebra is closed). A sequence of operations is an RA expression; its result is the answer to a query. RA matters because (1) it is the formal foundation of the relational model, (2) query processors translate SQL into RA trees and optimize them (Ch. 18–19), and (3) several of its ideas appear directly in SQL.

    RA is procedural: an expression fixes an order of operations. The relational calculus (§8.6–8.7, Topic 7) is declarative: it says only what to retrieve. The two have the same expressive power (§12).

    Set semantics

    In the formal model a relation is a set of tuples. Every RA result is therefore a set: π\piπ and ∪\cup∪ eliminate duplicates automatically, and tuple order means nothing. SQL tables are multisets (bags); that is why SQL needs DISTINCT. Inside an aggregate, however, duplicate values are not removed (SUM of 10, 10, 35 is 55).

    3  Unary operations: SELECT, PROJECT, RENAME · §8.1

    Theory recap

    SELECT (σ\sigmaσ)

    Definition: SELECT

    σ⟨selection condition⟩(R)\sigma_{\langle\text{selection condition}\rangle}(R)σ⟨selection condition⟩​(R) returns the tuples of RRR for which the condition is TRUE. The condition is a Boolean combination (and, or, not) of clauses attribute op constant or attribute op attribute, with op ∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\ne\}∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=} (=,≠=,\ne=,= only for unordered domains).

    • It is applied to each tuple independently, so a condition can never refer to two tuples (“salary greater than the salary of …” needs a join).
    • Degree of the result = degree of RRR (same attributes). Cardinality: ∣σc(R)∣≤∣R∣|\sigma_c(R)| \le |R|∣σc​(R)∣≤∣R∣.
    • Selectivity of ccc = fraction of tuples selected =∣σc(R)∣/∣R∣= |\sigma_c(R)|/|R|=∣σc​(R)∣/∣R∣.

    PROJECT (π\piπ)

    Definition: PROJECT

    π⟨attribute list⟩(R)\pi_{\langle\text{attribute list}\rangle}(R)π⟨attribute list⟩​(R) returns a relation with only the listed attributes, in the listed order, and with duplicate tuples eliminated.

    • Degree = number of attributes in the list. Cardinality: ∣πL(R)∣≤∣R∣|\pi_L(R)|\le|R|∣πL​(R)∣≤∣R∣; equality is guaranteed if LLL is a superkey of RRR (contains a key).
    • Duplicate elimination: πSex, Salary(EMPLOYEE)\pi_{\text{Sex, Salary}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})πSex, Salary​(EMPLOYEE) has 7 tuples, not 8, because ⟨\langle⟨F, 25000⟩\rangle⟩ occurs for Zelaya and English (Jabbar is ⟨\langle⟨M, 25000⟩\rangle⟩). It costs a sort or hash. Without it the result would be a bag; SQL keeps bags unless DISTINCT.
    • Cascade: πL1(πL2(R))=πL1(R)\pi_{L_1}(\pi_{L_2}(R))=\pi_{L_1}(R)πL1​​(πL2​​(R))=πL1​​(R) provided L1⊆L2L_1\subseteq L_2L1​⊆L2​; otherwise the left side is undefined. π\piπ is not commutative.

    Sequences of operations and RENAME (ρ\rhoρ)

    A query can be written in-line as one nested expression, or as a sequence of assignments to named intermediate relations with ←\leftarrow←. Both are equivalent:

    πFname, Lname, Salary(σDno=5(EMPLOYEE))\pi_{\text{Fname, Lname, Salary}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Dno=5}}\left(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\right)\right)πFname, Lname, Salary​(σDno=5​(EMPLOYEE))

    or, as a sequence,

    DEP5_EMPS  ←  σDno=5(EMPLOYEE)R(First_name, Last_name, Salary)  ←  πFname, Lname, Salary(DEP5_EMPS)\begin{array}{rcl} \mathit{DEP5\_EMPS} &\;\leftarrow\;& \sigma_{\text{Dno=5}}\left(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\right)\\ \mathit{R}(\text{First\_name, Last\_name, Salary}) &\;\leftarrow\;& \pi_{\text{Fname, Lname, Salary}}\left(\mathit{DEP5\_EMPS}\right) \end{array}DEP5_EMPSR(First_name, Last_name, Salary)​←←​σDno=5​(EMPLOYEE)πFname, Lname, Salary​(DEP5_EMPS)​

    Writing R(B1,…,Bn)←E\mathit{R}(B_1,\dots,B_n)\leftarrow ER(B1​,…,Bn​)←E renames the attributes positionally. The formal RENAME operator has three forms: ρS(B1,…,Bn)(R)\rho_{S(B_1,\dots,B_n)}(R)ρS(B1​,…,Bn​)​(R) (relation and attributes), ρS(R)\rho_S(R)ρS​(R) (relation only), ρ(B1,…,Bn)(R)\rho_{(B_1,\dots,B_n)}(R)ρ(B1​,…,Bn​)​(R) (attributes only). Without renaming, σ\sigmaσ keeps RRR’s attribute names, and π\piπ uses the names in its list. SQL renames with AS.

    When renaming is necessary

    (1) A self-join (two copies of one relation: employee and supervisor), otherwise every attribute name is ambiguous and a natural join of a relation with itself returns the relation; (2) before a natural join or division, so that exactly the intended attributes have the same name (e.g. Dnumber→\to→Dnum); (3) before ∪,∩,−\cup,\cap,-∪,∩,− when you want meaningful result names (the result takes the first operand’s names); (4) to name the output of an aggregate or a generalized projection.

    4  Set operations and the Cartesian product · §8.2

    Theory recap
    Definition: Union compatibility (type compatibility)

    R(A1,…,An)R(A_1,\dots,A_n)R(A1​,…,An​) and S(B1,…,Bn)S(B_1,\dots,B_n)S(B1​,…,Bn​) are union compatible if they have the same degree nnn and dom(Ai)=dom(Bi)\mathrm{dom}(A_i)=\mathrm{dom}(B_i)dom(Ai​)=dom(Bi​) for 1≤i≤n1\le i\le n1≤i≤n. Names need not match; the result uses the names of RRR.

    • R∪SR\cup SR∪S: tuples in RRR or SSS or both (duplicates eliminated). R∩SR\cap SR∩S: tuples in both. R−SR-SR−S: tuples in RRR not in SSS.
    • ∪\cup∪ and ∩\cap∩ are commutative and associative (so nnn-ary); −-− is neither: R−S≠S−RR-S\ne S-RR−S=S−R in general.
    • R∩S=((R∪S)−(R−S))−(S−R)=R−(R−S)R\cap S = ((R\cup S)-(R-S))-(S-R) = R-(R-S)R∩S=((R∪S)−(R−S))−(S−R)=R−(R−S).
    • Compatibility is needed because the operations compare whole tuples: a tuple of degree 3 can never equal a tuple of degree 2, comparing values from different domains (Ssn vs. Salary) is meaningless, and the result must itself be a relation with one schema.

    Why theta join is needed (Ex. 8.4)

    Equality covers FK–PK links, but many queries compare values with <,>,≠<,>,\ne<,>,=: “employees earning more than their supervisor” (E.Salary>S.SalaryE.\text{Salary}>S.\text{Salary}E.Salary>S.Salary after E.Super_ssn=S.SsnE.\text{Super\_ssn}=S.\text{Ssn}E.Super_ssn=S.Ssn), “pairs of different employees” (≠\ne=), “books published before a coauthor was born” (RA-G Q2(c)), and the “not the maximum” trick σS1<S2\sigma_{S_1<S_2}σS1​<S2​​. A natural join can only test equality of same-named attributes.

    Division traps

    (1) The divisor’s attributes must be exactly the attributes of the dividend you want matched: project WORKS_ON to (Essn, Pno) first; dividing all of WORKS_ON (with Hours) by a Pno-list would also require matching Hours. (2) Names must agree: rename Pnumber to Pno. (3) If the divisor is empty, every candidate qualifies (“for all” over an empty set is true); state this as an assumption if it can happen. (4) “works on some project of dept 5” is a join, “all projects” is division.

    7  Query trees · §8.3.5

    Theory recap

    A query tree represents an RA expression: leaves are input relations, internal nodes are operations, the root produces the result. An internal node executes when its children are available. It fixes an order of execution, which is why optimizers use it (Ch. 18–19). Query Q2: for every project located in Stafford, list the project number, controlling department number, and the manager’s last name, address and birth date:

    πPnumber, Dnum, Lname, Address, Bdate(((σPlocation=‘Stafford’(PROJECT))⋈Dnum=DnumberDEPARTMENT)⋈Mgr_ssn=SsnEMPLOYEE)\begin{gathered}\pi_{\text{Pnumber, Dnum, Lname, Address, Bdate}}\big(((\sigma_{\text{Plocation=`Stafford'}}(\textsf{PROJECT}))\\ \bowtie_{\text{Dnum=Dnumber}}\textsf{DEPARTMENT})\bowtie_{\text{Mgr\_ssn=Ssn}}\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\big)\end{gathered}πPnumber, Dnum, Lname, Address, Bdate​(((σPlocation=‘Stafford’​(PROJECT))⋈Dnum=Dnumber​DEPARTMENT)⋈Mgr_ssn=Ssn​EMPLOYEE)​

    Result on Figure 5.6: (10, 4, Wallace, 291 Berry, Bellaire, TX, 1941-06-20) and (30, 4, Wallace, …). A query graph (§8.6.5) is the order-free alternative: relation nodes, constant nodes, condition edges.

    Generalized projection

    πF1,…,Fn(R)\pi_{F_1,\dots,F_n}(R)πF1​,…,Fn​​(R) where each FiF_iFi​ is a function of attributes (arithmetic, constants). Name the outputs with ρ\rhoρ:

    REPORT←ρ(Ssn, Net_salary, Bonus, Tax)(πSsn, Salary−Deduction, 2000∗Years_service, 0.25∗Salary(EMPLOYEE))\mathit{REPORT}\leftarrow\rho_{(\text{Ssn, Net\_salary, Bonus, Tax})}\big(\pi_{\text{Ssn, Salary}-\text{Deduction},\ 2000*\text{Years\_service},\ 0.25*\text{Salary}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})\big)REPORT←ρ(Ssn, Net_salary, Bonus, Tax)​(πSsn, Salary−Deduction, 2000∗Years_service, 0.25∗Salary​(EMPLOYEE))

    Aggregate functions and grouping (I\mathfrak{I}I, “script F”)

    Definition: AGGREGATE FUNCTION operation

    ⟨grouping attributes⟩ I ⟨function list⟩ (R)\langle\text{grouping attributes}\rangle\ \mathfrak{I}\ \langle\text{function list}\rangle\,(R)⟨grouping attributes⟩ I ⟨function list⟩(R): partition RRR into groups of tuples with equal grouping values, apply each (function, attribute) pair (SUM, AVERAGE, MAXIMUM, MINIMUM, COUNT) to each group. Result: grouping attributes + one attribute per function; one tuple per group.

    • Naming: without renaming, result attributes are called FUNCTION_attribute (COUNT_Ssn, AVERAGE_Salary); rename with ρR(… )\rho_{R(\dots)}ρR(…)​.
    • No grouping attributes: the whole relation is one group; the result has exactly one tuple.
    • Duplicates are not eliminated inside a group (so SUM/AVERAGE mean what they should); NULLs are ignored by every function (COUNT AAA counts non-NULL AAA values). The result is a relation, not a number, so the algebra stays closed.
    • A selection on an aggregate value (SQL HAVING) is a σ\sigmaσ after I\mathfrak{I}I; a selection on base attributes (SQL WHERE) is a σ\sigmaσ before it.

    Projection before aggregation changes the answer

    Because π\piπ removes duplicates, Pno ISUM Hours(πPno, Hours(WORKS_ON)){}_{\text{Pno}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Hours}}\left(\pi_{\text{Pno, Hours}}(\textsf{WORKS\_ON})\right)Pno​ISUM Hours​(πPno, Hours​(WORKS_ON)) gives 45 for project 10 (the two 10.0-hour rows collapse) instead of the correct 55. Aggregate over a relation that still contains a key of the things being summed (here keep Essn). Conversely, count distinct = project first, then COUNT.

    Recursive closure

    Recursive relationships (supervision) need a join per level:

    SUPERVISION(Ssn1, Ssn2)←πSsn, Super_ssn(EMPLOYEE)BORG_SSN←πSsn(σFname=‘James’∧Lname=‘Borg’(EMPLOYEE))RESULT1(Ssn)←πSsn1(SUPERVISION⋈Ssn2=SsnBORG_SSN)={333445555, 987654321}RESULT2(Ssn)←πSsn1(SUPERVISION⋈Ssn2=SsnRESULT1)={5 others}RESULT←RESULT2∪RESULT1(7 tuples: everyone except Borg)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{SUPERVISION}(\text{Ssn1, Ssn2}) &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn, Super\_ssn}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}) \\ \mathit{BORG\_SSN} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn}}(\sigma_{\text{Fname=`James'}\wedge\text{Lname=`Borg'}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})) \\ \mathit{RESULT1}(\text{Ssn}) &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn1}}(\mathit{SUPERVISION}\bowtie_{\text{Ssn2=Ssn}}\mathit{BORG\_SSN}) \quad=\{333445555,\ 987654321\} \\ \mathit{RESULT2}(\text{Ssn}) &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn1}}(\mathit{SUPERVISION}\bowtie_{\text{Ssn2=Ssn}}\mathit{RESULT1})\quad=\{\text{5 others}\} \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \mathit{RESULT2}\cup \mathit{RESULT1}\quad(7\text{ tuples: everyone except Borg})\end{array}SUPERVISION(Ssn1, Ssn2)BORG_SSNRESULT1(Ssn)RESULT2(Ssn)RESULT​←←←←←​πSsn, Super_ssn​(EMPLOYEE)πSsn​(σFname=‘James’∧Lname=‘Borg’​(EMPLOYEE))πSsn1​(SUPERVISION⋈Ssn2=Ssn​BORG_SSN)={333445555, 987654321}πSsn1​(SUPERVISION⋈Ssn2=Ssn​RESULT1)={5 others}RESULT2∪RESULT1(7 tuples: everyone except Borg)​

    “Supervisees at all levels” cannot be written in basic RA unless the number of levels is known: it needs a loop (repeat until no new tuples; here level 3 is empty) or a transitive closure operator (SQL: WITH RECURSIVE).

    OUTER JOINs

    Inner joins drop tuples without a match (and tuples with NULL join attributes). Outer joins keep them, padding the other side’s attributes with NULL:

    • R⟕SR\mathbin{\text{⟕}} SR⟕S (left): every tuple of RRR appears; unmatched ones get NULLs for SSS’s attributes.
    • R⟖SR\mathbin{\text{⟖}} SR⟖S (right): every tuple of SSS appears.
    • R⟗SR\mathbin{\text{⟗}} SR⟗S (full): every tuple of both.
    Figure 8.12: every employee with the department he/she manages

Wong–Research, Wallace–Administration, Borg–Headquarters; the other five employees get Dname = NULL. (8 tuples; an inner join gives 3.)

    OUTER UNION

    For partially compatible R(X,Y)R(X,Y)R(X,Y) and S(X,Z)S(X,Z)S(X,Z): result T(X,Y,Z)T(X,Y,Z)T(X,Y,Z); tuples that agree on XXX are merged into one; others are padded with NULL. It equals a full outer (natural) join on the common attributes XXX. Example: STUDENT(Name, Ssn, Department, Advisor) and INSTRUCTOR(Name, Ssn, Department, Rank) give

    STUDENT_OR_INSTRUCTOR(Name, Ssn, Department, Advisor, Rank);

    a student who also teaches in the same department appears once with all values. Plain ∪\cup∪ would be undefined here (degrees differ).

    NULL patterns in nested natural left outer joins

    2025 End-Sem Q8 (5 marks)

    r(A,B)r(A,B)r(A,B), s(B,C)s(B,C)s(B,C), t(B,D)t(B,D)t(B,D), all attributes NOT NULL.  E1 =r⟕(s⟕t)=r\mathbin{\text{⟕}}(s\mathbin{\text{⟕}} t)=r⟕(s⟕t),  E2 =(r⟕s)⟕t=(r\mathbin{\text{⟕}} s)\mathbin{\text{⟕}} t=(r⟕s)⟕t (natural). (a) Instance where E2 has C NULL but D non-NULL. (b) Is that possible in E1?

    (a) r={(1,10)}r=\{(1,10)\}r={(1,10)}, s={(20,5)}s=\{(20,5)\}s={(20,5)}, t={(10,100)}t=\{(10,100)\}t={(10,100)}. r⟕sr\mathbin{\text{⟕}} sr⟕s: B=10 has no match in sss ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ (1,10,NULL)(1,10,\textsf{NULL})(1,10,NULL). Joining with ttt is on B only (C is not in ttt), and B=10 matches ttt ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ E2 ={(A=1,B=10,C=NULL,D=100)}=\{(A{=}1,B{=}10,C{=}\textsf{NULL},D{=}100)\}={(A=1,B=10,C=NULL,D=100)}.

    (b) No. In u=s⟕tu=s\mathbin{\text{⟕}} tu=s⟕t every tuple comes from a tuple of sss, so its C is never NULL (C is NOT NULL in sss). In r⟕ur\mathbin{\text{⟕}} ur⟕u (join on B), a tuple of rrr either matches some tuple of uuu, and then C is copied from uuu and is non-NULL, or matches none, and then all of uuu’s attributes, C and D, are NULL. Hence C NULL ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ D NULL in E1. (On the instance above E1 ={(1,10,NULL,NULL)}=\{(1,10,\textsf{NULL},\textsf{NULL})\}={(1,10,NULL,NULL)}; a brute-force check over 3000 random instances found no counterexample.)

    Lessons

    Outer joins are not associative. In a left-deep chain (r⟕s)⟕t(r\mathbin{\text{⟕}} s)\mathbin{\text{⟕}} t(r⟕s)⟕t, a later relation can still match through attributes of rrr, so NULL patterns “mix”; in r⟕(s⟕t)r\mathbin{\text{⟕}}(s\mathbin{\text{⟕}} t)r⟕(s⟕t) the right operand is matched as a block, so its attributes are NULL all together or come from a real sss tuple.

    Evaluating an RA expression on small relations

    Method

    Rename clashing attributes (write R.B, S.B), evaluate innermost first, write each intermediate table with its schema, apply selections tuple by tuple, project with duplicate removal, and finish with the schema and the set of tuples. Graders want both.

    Equivalences and valid rewrites

    Two expressions are equivalent if they give the same result on every database state. Main rules (Ch. 19 uses them for optimization; “attrs” = attributes):

    1. Cascade / commute of σ\sigmaσ: σc1∧c2(R)=σc1(σc2(R))=σc2(σc1(R))\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2}(R)=\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R))=\sigma_{c_2}(\sigma_{c_1}(R))σc1​∧c2​​(R)=σc1​​(σc2​​(R))=σc2​​(σc1​​(R)).
    2. Cascade of π\piπ: πL1(πL2(R))=πL1(R)\pi_{L_1}(\pi_{L_2}(R))=\pi_{L_1}(R)πL1​​(πL2​​(R))=πL1​​(R) if L1⊆L2L_1\subseteq L_2L1​⊆L2​ (else undefined).
    3. σ\sigmaσ and π\piπ commute if ccc uses only attrs in LLL: πL(σc(R))=σc(πL(R))\pi_L(\sigma_c(R))=\sigma_c(\pi_L(R))πL​(σc​(R))=σc​(πL​(R)).
    4. ⋈\bowtie⋈, ×\times×, ∪\cup∪, ∩\cap∩ are commutative and associative (up to the order of columns); −-− is neither. Outer joins: R⟕S=S⟖RR\mathbin{\text{⟕}} S=S\mathbin{\text{⟖}} RR⟕S=S⟖R, but outer joins are not associative in general (previous subsection).
    5. Push σ\sigmaσ through ⋈\bowtie⋈/×\times×: if ccc uses only RRR’s attrs, σc(R⋈S)=σc(R)⋈S\sigma_c(R\bowtie S)=\sigma_c(R)\bowtie Sσc​(R⋈S)=σc​(R)⋈S; if c=c1∧c2c=c_1\wedge c_2c=c1​∧c2​ with c1c_1c1​ on RRR, c2c_2c2​ on SSS: σc(R⋈S)=σc1(R)⋈σc2(S)\sigma_c(R\bowtie S)=\sigma_{c_1}(R)\bowtie\sigma_{c_2}(S)σc​(R⋈S)=σc1​​(R)⋈σc2​​(S). For R⟕SR\mathbin{\text{⟕}} SR⟕S only a condition on the preserved side RRR may be pushed.
    6. σ\sigmaσ over ×\times× becomes a join: σc(R×S)=R⋈cS\sigma_c(R\times S)=R\bowtie_c Sσc​(R×S)=R⋈c​S.
    7. Push π\piπ through ⋈\bowtie⋈: πL(R⋈cS)=πL(πLR(R)⋈cπLS(S))\pi_L(R\bowtie_c S)=\pi_L(\pi_{L_R}(R)\bowtie_c\pi_{L_S}(S))πL​(R⋈c​S)=πL​(πLR​​(R)⋈c​πLS​​(S)) where LRL_RLR​, LSL_SLS​ are LLL’s attrs of each side plus the join attributes.

    10. σ\sigmaσ and aggregation: a condition on grouping attributes can move below I\mathfrak{I}I; a condition on an aggregate value cannot.

    11  Writing RA queries the way they are graded

    Theory recap
    RA query-writing method
    1. State assumptions with a reason: keys, FKs, NULLs, ties, empty sets (“a book with no coauthors is included, because a universal condition over an empty set is true”), how an ambiguous phrase is read.
    2. Identify the relations that hold the needed facts and the output attributes.
    3. Find the join paths: follow FK →\to→ PK links; write the condition (⋈Dno=Dnumber\bowtie_{\text{Dno=Dnumber}}⋈Dno=Dnumber​) or rename so a natural join matches exactly the intended attributes. Two roles of one relation (employee/supervisor, earlier/later book) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ two renamed copies.
    4. Apply selections (constants, comparisons) as early as possible; keep all conditions that must refer to the same combination in one selection over one combined relation.
    5. Project at the end to exactly the requested attributes (“complete rows” = all attributes of that relation). Keep a key until the end if names could collide.
    6. Name every intermediate result (TEMP←…\mathit{TEMP}\leftarrow\dotsTEMP←…) and explain each step in one line.

    Patterns. For all / every: division, or double negation: candidates −-− π((candidates×required)−actual)\pi(\text{(candidates}\times\text{required)}-\text{actual})π((candidates×required)−actual). None / no: πkey(all)−πkey(those with)\pi_{\text{key}}(\text{all})-\pi_{\text{key}}(\text{those with})πkey​(all)−πkey​(those with). At least two: self-join of renamed copies with equal owner and different item, e.g. πE1(σE1=E2 ∧ P1≠P2(ρ(E1,P1)(W)×ρ(E2,P2)(W)))\pi_{\text{E1}}(\sigma_{E1=E2\,\wedge\,P1\ne P2}(\rho_{(E1,P1)}(W)\times\rho_{(E2,P2)}(W)))πE1​(σE1=E2∧P1=P2​(ρ(E1,P1)​(W)×ρ(E2,P2)​(W))), or I\mathfrak{I}I COUNT then σ≥2\sigma_{\ge2}σ≥2​. Maximum without I\mathfrak{I}I: πkey(R)−πR1.key(σR1.v<R2.v(R1×R2))\pi_{\text{key}}(R)-\pi_{R_1.\text{key}}(\sigma_{R_1.v<R_2.v}(R_1\times R_2))πkey​(R)−πR1​.key​(σR1​.v<R2​.v​(R1​×R2​)) (those beaten by someone are not the max). Per-group counts with zero: left outer join to the groups, then COUNT of a right-side attribute (COUNT ignores NULL).

    How RA answers are graded (Moodle RA-I / RA-G rubrics)
    • Marks go to what the expression computes; an equivalent expression gets full marks. Any standard notation is accepted (γ\gammaγ or GIF_G\mathfrak{I}_FG​IF​, ∗*∗ or ⋈\bowtie⋈, σc(R×S)\sigma_c(R\times S)σc​(R×S) for R⋈cSR\bowtie_c SR⋈c​S). Named steps ending in the answer count as one expression; earlier steps may be reused.
    • Each part has an assumption mark (about 1 of 5): stated with a reason; half if one is missing or reasons are absent. Unstated readings are graded against what the expression does, losing only that mark; readings outside the accepted list get nothing.
    • A mistake is penalised once. Slips that do not change meaning (missing bracket, ∗\ast∗ for ⋈\bowtie⋈) are free.
    • Undefined expressions score 0 for that criterion: ∪\cup∪/−-− on non-union-compatible relations, an ambiguous attribute, an attribute not in the relation (e.g. selecting on a projected-away attribute).
    • Relations are sets: π\piπ removes duplicates, so COUNT after a projection counts distinct values.
    • Two answers with neither marked final: the weaker is graded. Half marks only where the rubric lists them.
    • Typical deductions: natural join of relations with no common attribute name (a Cartesian product) instead of ⋈AuthorName=Name\bowtie_{\text{AuthorName=Name}}⋈AuthorName=Name​; not renaming the two copies in a self-join; an existential test where “all” is asked (e.g. >>> MIN instead of >>> MAX), which scores 0 for that criterion; grouping on a non-key (Title) that merges different objects; counting after a join that multiplies rows; non-strict comparison where “before/younger” is strict; testing correlated conditions in separate sub-expressions combined only through a name; returning only some attributes when “complete rows” are asked.

    12  Relational calculus in brief · §8.6, for Ex. 8.9–8.12

    Theory recap

    Full treatment is in Topic 7; this is what the review questions need.

    • Tuple relational calculus (TRC): variables range over tuples; form {t1.Aj,⋯∣COND(t1,…,tn+m)}\{t_1.A_j,\dots \mid \text{COND}(t_1,\dots,t_{n+m})\}{t1​.Aj​,⋯∣COND(t1​,…,tn+m​)}. {t∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}\{t \mid \textsf{EMPLOYEE}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\text{Salary}>50000\}{t∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}.
    • Range relation: R(t)R(t)R(t) says ttt ranges over RRR. Atoms: R(t)R(t)R(t); ti.A op tj.Bt_i.A\ \text{op}\ t_j.Bti​.A op tj​.B; ti.A op ct_i.A\ \text{op}\ cti​.A op c. Formulas: atoms combined by and, or, not and quantifiers (∃t)(\exists t)(∃t), (∀t)(\forall t)(∀t). A variable is free unless quantified (bound); only the variables left of ∣\mid∣ may be free.
    • Domain relational calculus (DRC): variables range over attribute values; form {x1,…,xn∣COND}\{x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\text{COND}\}{x1​,…,xn​∣COND}; atoms R(x1…xj)R(x_1\dots x_j)R(x1​…xj​), xi op xjx_i\ \text{op}\ x_jxi​ op xj​, xi op cx_i\ \text{op}\ cxi​ op c. QBE is based on it.
    • (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F) is TRUE if FFF holds for at least one tuple; (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F) if it holds for every tuple in the universe, so write (∀x)(not R(x)or… )(\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, R(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\dots)(∀x)(notR(x)or…) to exclude irrelevant tuples. (∀x)P(x)≡not (∃x)(not P(x))(\forall x)P(x)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x))(∀x)P(x)≡not(∃x)(notP(x)).
    • A safe expression returns only values from its domain (finite result); {t∣not EMPLOYEE(t)}\{t\mid \textbf{not}\, \textsf{EMPLOYEE}(t)\}{t∣notEMPLOYEE(t)} is unsafe.
    • Basic RA and safe TRC/DRC have the same expressive power; a language that can express every relational-calculus query is relationally complete. Calculus is declarative (no order); RA is procedural. Neither basic language has aggregates.

    13  Chapter 7 exercises in relational algebra

    Textbook exercises

    Why Chapter 7 appears under Relational Algebra

    The course lists 7.1–7.9 under Relational Algebra, but in the 7th edition Chapter 7 is “More SQL”. The SQL document (Topic 8) solves 7.1–7.9 fully in SQL. Here: 7.1–7.4 are answered briefly through their RA counterparts (see Topic 8 for the full SQL answer); 7.5–7.7 are written in relational algebra with named steps and checked on Figure 5.6 / Figure 1.2; 7.8–7.9 express each view as an RA expression. Every query below was evaluated with a small Python RA engine on the instance; the result tables are its output.

    7.1The six clauses of an SQL queryE&N Ex. 7.1 · p. 236

    Describe the six clauses in the syntax of an SQL retrieval query. Show what type of constructs can be specified in each of the six clauses. Which of the six clauses are required and which are optional?

    Solution · written for this guide
    ClauseConstructs allowedRA counterpartRequired?
    SELECTattribute list, *, DISTINCT, expressions, aggregate functions, ASπ\piπ (generalized), ρ\rhoρyes
    FROMtables, aliases, joined tables (JOIN … ON, NATURAL, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER), subqueries×\times×, ⋈\bowtie⋈, ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕, ρ\rhoρyes
    WHEREconditions with comparisons, AND/OR/NOT, LIKE, BETWEEN, IS NULL, IN, EXISTS, nested queriesσ\sigmaσ (and −-−, ÷\div÷ for NOT EXISTS)optional
    GROUP BYgrouping attributesgrouping part of GI_G\mathfrak{I}G​Ioptional
    HAVINGcondition on groups (aggregates)σ\sigmaσ applied after I\mathfrak{I}Ioptional (needs grouping)
    ORDER BYattributes/positions with ASC/DESCnone (relations are unordered)optional
    Answer

    SELECT and FROM are required; WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY are optional. A full query corresponds to πL(σHAVING(GIF(σWHERE(R1×⋯×Rn))))\pi_{L}\big(\sigma_{\text{HAVING}}\big({}_{G}\mathfrak{I}_{F}\big(\sigma_{\text{WHERE}}(R_1\times\dots\times R_n)\big)\big)\big)πL​(σHAVING​(G​IF​(σWHERE​(R1​×⋯×Rn​)))) followed by sorting. Full SQL answer: Topic 8.

    7.2Conceptual evaluation orderE&N Ex. 7.2 · p. 236★ Must-do

    Describe conceptually how an SQL retrieval query will be executed by specifying the conceptual order of executing each of the six clauses.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Read the RA expression of 7.1 from the inside out:

    1. FROM: form the Cartesian product / joins of the listed tables (×\times×, ⋈\bowtie⋈).
    2. WHERE: keep the combined tuples that make the condition TRUE (σ\sigmaσ), tuple by tuple.
    3. GROUP BY: partition the remaining tuples into groups (the grouping part of I\mathfrak{I}I).
    4. HAVING: keep the groups whose aggregate condition is TRUE (σ\sigmaσ over the output of I\mathfrak{I}I).
    5. SELECT: compute the output columns and aggregates (π\piπ / generalized π\piπ); DISTINCT removes duplicates (RA’s π\piπ always does).
    6. ORDER BY: sort the result (no RA counterpart).
    Answer

    FROM →\to→ WHERE →\to→ GROUP BY →\to→ HAVING →\to→ SELECT →\to→ ORDER BY. Consequence: a WHERE condition cannot use an aggregate (groups do not exist yet), and a SELECT alias cannot be used in WHERE. Real optimizers may reorder (pushing σ\sigmaσ down) only into an equivalent RA expression.

    7.3NULLs in comparisons, aggregates and groupingE&N Ex. 7.3 · p. 236★ Must-do

    Discuss how NULLs are treated in comparison operators in SQL. How are NULLs treated when aggregate functions are applied in an SQL query? How are NULLs treated if they exist in grouping attributes?

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Comparisons: any comparison with NULL (even NULL = NULL) is UNKNOWN; SQL uses three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN: AND takes the minimum, OR the maximum, NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN). WHERE keeps only TRUE tuples. Test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. RA: σ\sigmaσ also selects only tuples whose condition is TRUE, and a join never matches on a NULL join attribute. Example: σSuper_ssn≠‘333445555’(EMPLOYEE)\sigma_{\text{Super\_ssn}\ne\text{`333445555'}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})σSuper_ssn=‘333445555’​(EMPLOYEE) does not return Borg (Super_ssn NULL).
    • Aggregates: NULLs are discarded before the function is applied; COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(A) counts non-NULL AAA; on an empty (or all-NULL) collection SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN return NULL and COUNT returns 0. RA: I\mathfrak{I}I ignores NULLs in the same way. Example: for project 20, Hours ={10,15,NULL}=\{10, 15, \text{NULL}\}={10,15,NULL}: SUM = 25, COUNT Hours = 2, COUNT Essn = 3, AVERAGE = 12.5 (not 25/3).
    • Grouping: all tuples with NULL in the grouping attribute form one separate group. Example: grouping EMPLOYEE on Super_ssn gives a group for NULL containing Borg.
    Answer

    Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN and fail WHERE/σ\sigmaσ/joins; aggregates skip NULLs (except COUNT(*)); NULL grouping values form one group. Full SQL answer: Topic 8.

    7.4SQL constructsE&N Ex. 7.4 · p. 236

    Discuss how each of the following constructs is used in SQL, and discuss the various options for each construct. Specify what each construct is useful for. a. Nested queries. b. Joined tables and outer joins. c. Aggregate functions and grouping. d. Triggers. e. Assertions and how they differ from triggers. f. The SQL WITH clause. g. SQL CASE construct. h. Views and their updatability. i. Schema change commands.

    Solution · written for this guide
    ConstructUse and options (SQL)RA view
    a. Nested queriessubquery in WHERE with IN, op ANY/SOME/ALL, EXISTS/NOT EXISTS; correlated or not; also in FROM/SELECTIN/EXISTS = join (semi-join) + π\piπ; NOT IN/NOT EXISTS = difference; “for all” (NOT EXISTS … EXCEPT) = division
    b. Joined tables, outer joinsJOIN … ON, NATURAL JOIN, CROSS JOIN, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN; separates join conditions from WHERE⋈c\bowtie_c⋈c​, ∗\mathbin{*}∗, ×\times×, ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕, ⟖\mathbin{\text{⟖}}⟖, ⟗\mathbin{\text{⟗}}⟗
    c. Aggregates, groupingCOUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN; GROUP BY; HAVING; DISTINCT inside aggregatesGIF_G\mathfrak{I}_FG​IF​; σ\sigmaσ after it for HAVING
    d. TriggersECA rules: CREATE TRIGGER … BEFORE/AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE … FOR EACH ROW WHEN …; monitoring, derived valuesnone (not a query)
    e. AssertionsCREATE ASSERTION … CHECK (NOT EXISTS (…)): a state constraint that must always hold; the DBMS rejects violating updates; a trigger reacts with an actionthe CHECK body is a query whose RA result must be empty
    f. WITHnames a temporary table for one query; WITH RECURSIVE for transitive closureexactly the named intermediate relation T←E\mathit{T}\leftarrow ET←E; recursion = closure (not in basic RA)
    g. CASEvalue chosen by conditions, in SELECT/UPDATE/WHEREgeneralized projection with a conditional function
    h. ViewsCREATE VIEW: a virtual table defined by a query; updatable if it is a single-table view containing a key and no aggregates/DISTINCT/grouping; WITH CHECK OPTIONa named RA expression; updatable only if the update can be translated uniquely back through the expression
    i. Schema changeDROP TABLE/SCHEMA … CASCADE/RESTRICT; ALTER TABLE … ADD/DROP COLUMN, ADD/DROP CONSTRAINT, ALTER … SET DEFAULTnone (DDL)

    7.5Department aggregates (COMPANY)E&N Ex. 7.5 · p. 236

    Specify the following queries on the database in Figure 5.5 in SQL [here: in relational algebra]. Show the query results if each query is applied to the database state in Figure 5.6. a. For each department whose average employee salary is more than $30,000, retrieve the department name and the number of employees working for that department. b. Suppose that we want the number of male employees in each department making more than $30,000, rather than all employees (as in Exercise 7.5a). Can we specify this query in SQL? Why or why not?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Employees working for a department” are the EMPLOYEE tuples with that Dno. Why: Dno is the FK that records the department an employee works for.
    2. Every employee has a non-NULL Ssn (the key), so COUNT Ssn counts employees. Why: entity integrity.
    3. (b) is read as in the book: departments are still chosen by the average salary of all their employees (>>> $30,000, as in (a)), and for each such department we count the male employees earning more than $30,000; a department with none shows 0. Why: “rather than all employees” changes only what is counted.

    (a)

    T(Dno, No_emps, Avg_sal)←Dno ICOUNT Ssn, AVERAGE Salary(EMPLOYEE)H←σAvg_sal>30000(T)RESULT_A←πDname, No_emps(H⋈Dno=DnumberDEPARTMENT)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{T}(\text{Dno, No\_emps, Avg\_sal}) &\leftarrow& {}_{\text{Dno}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Ssn, AVERAGE Salary}}\left(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\right) \\ \mathit{H} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Avg\_sal$>$30000}}\left(\mathit{T}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT\_A} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dname, No\_emps}}\left(\mathit{H}\bowtie_{\text{Dno=Dnumber}}\textsf{DEPARTMENT}\right)\end{array}T(Dno, No_emps, Avg_sal)HRESULT_A​←←←​Dno​ICOUNT Ssn, AVERAGE Salary​(EMPLOYEE)σAvg_sal>30000​(T)πDname, No_emps​(H⋈Dno=Dnumber​DEPARTMENT)​

    T={(5,4,33250),(4,3,31000),(1,1,55000)}\mathit{T}=\{(5,4,33250),(4,3,31000),(1,1,55000)\}T={(5,4,33250),(4,3,31000),(1,1,55000)}: all three averages exceed 30000. The condition on the average is a σ\sigmaσ after I\mathfrak{I}I (SQL HAVING).

    DnameNo_emps
    Research4
    Administration3
    Headquarters1

    (b)

    In SQL, putting Sex=’M’ AND Salary>30000 in WHERE would also change the average used to choose the departments (WHERE runs before GROUP BY), so the one-block query of (a) cannot be reused; it needs a nested query or two aggregations. In RA the two computations are separate:

    HD←πDno(H)(departments chosen in (a))M←πDno, Ssn(σSex=‘M’ ∧ Salary>30000(EMPLOYEE))C(Dno, No_male_high)←Dno ICOUNT Ssn(HD⟕M)RESULT_B←πDname, No_male_high(C⋈Dno=DnumberDEPARTMENT)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{HD} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dno}}\left(\mathit{H}\right)\quad\text{(departments chosen in (a))} \\ \mathit{M} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dno, Ssn}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Sex=`M' $\wedge$ Salary$>$30000}}\left(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{C}(\text{Dno, No\_male\_high}) &\leftarrow& {}_{\text{Dno}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Ssn}}\left(\mathit{HD}\mathbin{\text{⟕}}\mathit{M}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT\_B} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dname, No\_male\_high}}\left(\mathit{C}\bowtie_{\text{Dno=Dnumber}}\textsf{DEPARTMENT}\right)\end{array}HDMC(Dno, No_male_high)RESULT_B​←←←←​πDno​(H)(departments chosen in (a))πDno, Ssn​(σSex=‘M’ ∧ Salary>30000​(EMPLOYEE))Dno​ICOUNT Ssn​(HD⟕M)πDname, No_male_high​(C⋈Dno=Dnumber​DEPARTMENT)​

    M={(5,333445555),(5,666884444),(1,888665555)}\mathit{M}=\{(5,333445555),(5,666884444),(1,888665555)\}M={(5,333445555),(5,666884444),(1,888665555)}. The natural left outer join on Dno keeps department 4 as (4,NULL)(4,\textsf{NULL})(4,NULL), and COUNT Ssn ignores the NULL, giving 0.

    DnameNo_male_high
    Research2
    Administration0
    Headquarters1
    Answer

    (a) Research 4, Administration 3, Headquarters 1. (b) Yes, it can be specified, but not by adding the conditions to the WHERE clause of (a); the department condition and the count must be computed separately (nested query in SQL; two aggregates joined, as above, in RA). Result: Research 2, Administration 0, Headquarters 1.

    What the grader checks

    Grouping on Dno (a key of the groups), the average condition applied after aggregation, Dname obtained by a join on Dno=Dnumber (a natural join of T\mathit{T}T and DEPARTMENT has no common attribute and would be a Cartesian product). In (b) the classic error is filtering before computing the average.

    7.7Nested-query style questions (COMPANY)E&N Ex. 7.7 · p. 237★ Must-do

    In SQL [here: in relational algebra], specify the following queries on the database in Figure 5.5 using the concept of nested queries and other concepts described in this chapter. a. Retrieve the names of all employees who work in the department that has the employee with the highest salary among all employees. b. Retrieve the names of all employees whose supervisor’s supervisor has ‘888665555’ for Ssn. c. Retrieve the names of employees who make at least $10,000 more than the employee who is paid the least in the company.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Names” = (Fname, Lname). Why: as in the book’s examples.
    2. (a) If several employees share the highest salary, the departments of all of them qualify. Why: “the employee with the highest salary” does not break ties.
    3. (c) “At least $10,000 more” means Salary ≥\ge≥ minimum +++ 10000. Why: “at least” includes equality.

    Consider the following view, DEPT_SUMMARY, defined on the COMPANY database in Figure 5.6:

    enowould mean deleting all employees of large departments, which is not what deleting a summary row means; aggregate views are not updatablerejected (no group has C >>> 4 anyway)

    (a), (b), (c) are allowed, with results: all three summary rows; (5, 4); (5, 33250). (d) and (e) are not allowed, because the view is defined with grouping and aggregate functions and the updates have no unique translation to EMPLOYEE.

    8.2Union compatibilityE&N Ex. 8.2 · p. 280

    What is union compatibility? Why do the UNION, INTERSECTION, and DIFFERENCE operations require that the relations on which they are applied be union compatible?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definition. R(A1,…,An)R(A_1,\dots,A_n)R(A1​,…,An​) and S(B1,…,Bn)S(B_1,\dots,B_n)S(B1​,…,Bn​) are union (type) compatible if they have the same degree nnn and dom(Ai)=dom(Bi)\mathrm{dom}(A_i)=\mathrm{dom}(B_i)dom(Ai​)=dom(Bi​) for 1≤i≤n1\le i\le n1≤i≤n.

    Why. (1) The three operations compare whole tuples for equality; tuples of different degrees or with values from different domains can never meaningfully be equal. (2) The result must be a relation with a single schema; if the operands’ iii-th columns had different domains, the result’s iii-th column would mix (say) Ssns and salaries.

    Worked Example

    πSsn(EMPLOYEE)−πEssn(DEPENDENT)\pi_{\text{Ssn}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})-\pi_{\text{Essn}}(\textsf{DEPENDENT})πSsn​(EMPLOYEE)−πEssn​(DEPENDENT) is valid (both 1 attribute of Ssn domain; the result is called Ssn). πSsn(EMPLOYEE)∪πEssn, Dependent_name(DEPENDENT)\pi_{\text{Ssn}}(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})\cup\pi_{\text{Essn, Dependent\_name}}(\textsf{DEPENDENT})πSsn​(EMPLOYEE)∪πEssn, Dependent_name​(DEPENDENT) is undefined (degrees 1 and 2) and scores 0 in a graded query.

    8.4Kinds of inner join; why theta joinE&N Ex. 8.4 · p. 280★ Must-do

    Discuss the various types of inner join operations. Why is theta join required?

    Solution · written for this guide

    An inner join combines a tuple of RRR with a tuple of SSS only when they satisfy the join condition; unmatched tuples (and NULL join values) are dropped. Formally R⋈cS=σc(R×S)R\bowtie_c S=\sigma_c(R\times S)R⋈c​S=σc​(R×S).

    TypeConditionResult attributesExample on Fig. 5.6
    Theta join R⋈cSR\bowtie_c SR⋈c​Sconjunction of Ai θ BjA_i\,\theta\,B_jAi​θBj​, θ∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\theta\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\ne\}θ∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=}all n+mn+mn+memployees paid more than their supervisor
    Equijoinonly ===all n+mn+mn+m; join-attribute pairs identicalDEPARTMENT⋈Mgr_ssn=SsnEMPLOYEE\textsf{DEPARTMENT}\bowtie_{\text{Mgr\_ssn=Ssn}}\textsf{EMPLOYEE}DEPARTMENT⋈Mgr_ssn=Ssn​EMPLOYEE (3 tuples, Mgr_ssn = Ssn in each)
    Natural join R∗SR\mathbin{*} SR∗S=== on every pair of same-named attributescommon attributes onceDEPARTMENT∗DEPT_LOCATIONS\textsf{DEPARTMENT}\mathbin{*}\textsf{DEPT\_LOCATIONS}DEPARTMENT∗DEPT_LOCATIONS (5 tuples)

    Related: a join with no condition is the Cartesian product; joins can be chained (nnn-way) and a relation can be joined with (a renamed copy of) itself. Join selectivity = expected result size / (nRnS)(n_R n_S)(nR​nS​).

    Why theta join is required. Equijoin and natural join can express only equality matches, but many queries relate tuples by order or inequality:

    • employees earning more than their supervisor:

      ρE(EMPLOYEE)⋈E.Super_ssn=S.Ssn ∧ E.Salary>S.SalaryρS(EMPLOYEE)\rho_E(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})\bowtie_{E.\text{Super\_ssn}=S.\text{Ssn}\,\wedge\,E.\text{Salary}>S.\text{Salary}}\rho_S(\textsf{EMPLOYEE})ρE​(EMPLOYEE)⋈E.Super_ssn=S.Ssn∧E.Salary>S.Salary​ρS​(EMPLOYEE)

      (on Fig. 5.6: none, since every employee earns less than his/her supervisor);

    • “not the maximum”: πSsn1(E1⋈Sal1<Sal2E2)\pi_{\text{Ssn1}}(E_1\bowtie_{\text{Sal1}<\text{Sal2}}E_2)πSsn1​(E1​⋈Sal1<Sal2​E2​), the basic-RA way to find a maximum;
    • band/range conditions: R⋈R.B≥S.CSR\bowtie_{R.B\ge S.C}SR⋈R.B≥S.C​S (2025 End-Sem Q5), “published before the coauthor was born” (RA-G).

    It is also the general form: equijoin and natural join are special cases, and every join is a theta join over a Cartesian product.

    Answer

    Inner joins: theta join (any comparison), equijoin (only ===), natural join (equijoin on same-named attributes with duplicates removed). Theta join is needed because many queries match tuples by <,≤,>,≥,≠<,\le,>,\ge,\ne<,≤,>,≥,=, which equality joins cannot express; the others are special cases of it.

    What the grader checks

    Name all three, give the condition and the result schema of each (natural join keeps one copy), and an example where θ≠=\theta\ne{=}θ== is essential.

    8.5Foreign keys and meaningful joinsE&N Ex. 8.5 · p. 281

    What role does the concept of foreign key play when specifying the most common types of meaningful join operations?

    Solution · written for this guide

    The meaningful joins in a schema are almost always FK = PK equijoins: a foreign key records exactly which tuple of the referenced relation a tuple is related to, so the join condition is “FK attribute = referenced key”.

    • The FK tells you the join path: EMPLOYEE.Dno = DEPARTMENT.Dnumber, DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn = EMPLOYEE.Ssn, WORKS_ON.Pno = PROJECT.Pnumber.
    • Because the referenced side is a key, each referencing tuple matches at most one tuple; with referential integrity and a non-NULL FK, exactly one. So ∣EMPLOYEE⋈Dno=DnumberDEPARTMENT∣=∣EMPLOYEE∣=8|\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\bowtie_{\text{Dno=Dnumber}}\textsf{DEPARTMENT}|=|\textsf{EMPLOYEE}|=8∣EMPLOYEE⋈Dno=Dnumber​DEPARTMENT∣=∣EMPLOYEE∣=8; no tuples lost or multiplied.
    • A tuple whose FK is NULL (Borg’s Super_ssn) drops out of the inner join; use an outer join to keep it.
    • Joining on attributes that are not an FK–key pair (e.g. Plocation = Dlocation) is legal but usually multiplies tuples and has no clear meaning; a natural join on attributes that merely share a name, or with no shared name at all (a Cartesian product), is a classic error.

    8.10Existential and universal quantifiersE&N Ex. 8.10 · p. 281★ Must-do

    Discuss the meanings of the existential quantifier (∃\exists∃) and the universal quantifier (∀\forall∀).

    Solution · written for this guide
    • (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F) is TRUE if FFF is TRUE for at least one tuple assigned to ttt; otherwise FALSE. It expresses “some”, “there is”, “at least one”, and is the calculus counterpart of a join/projection in RA. Q7: managers with some dependent: (∃d)(∃p)(DEPARTMENT(d)andDEPENDENT(p)ande.Ssn=d.Mgr_ssnandp.Essn=e.Ssn)(\exists d)(\exists p)(\textsf{DEPARTMENT}(d)\mathbin{\textbf{and}}\textsf{DEPENDENT}(p)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} e.\text{Ssn}=d.\text{Mgr\_ssn}\mathbin{\textbf{and}} p.\text{Essn}=e.\text{Ssn})(∃d)(∃p)(DEPARTMENT(d)andDEPENDENT(p)ande.Ssn=d.Mgr_ssnandp.Essn=e.Ssn).
    • (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F) is TRUE if FFF is TRUE for every tuple in the universe assigned to ttt. Because ttt ranges over all tuples, we must make FFF trivially true for the tuples we do not care about: (∀x)(not PROJECT(x)ornot (x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(… ))(\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, \textsf{PROJECT}(x)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, (x.\text{Dnum}=5)\mathbin{\textbf{or}}(\exists w)(\dots))(∀x)(notPROJECT(x)ornot(x.Dnum=5)or(∃w)(…)) (Q3: works on all dept-5 projects). It is the counterpart of RA division.
    • A quantifier binds its variable; unquantified variables are free and only those may appear left of the bar.
    • They are interchangeable via negation: (∀x)P(x)≡not (∃x)(not P(x))(\forall x)P(x)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x))(∀x)P(x)≡not(∃x)(notP(x)) and (∃x)P(x)≡not (∀x)(not P(x))(\exists x)P(x)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\forall x)(\textbf{not}\, P(x))(∃x)P(x)≡not(∀x)(notP(x)); with connectives, AND and OR swap: (∀x)(PandQ)≡not (∃x)(not Pornot Q)(\forall x)(P\mathbin{\textbf{and}} Q)\equiv \textbf{not}\, (\exists x)(\textbf{not}\, P\mathbin{\textbf{or}}\textbf{not}\, Q)(∀x)(PandQ)≡not(∃x)(notPornotQ). Also (∀x)P(x)⇒(∃x)P(x)(\forall x)P(x)\Rightarrow(\exists x)P(x)(∀x)P(x)⇒(∃x)P(x) (for a non-empty universe).
    • “All” over an empty set is TRUE (vacuous truth); “exists” over an empty set is FALSE. This is the source of many stated assumptions (RA-I A5).
    Answer

    ∃\exists∃: true if some tuple satisfies the formula; ∀\forall∀: true if every tuple in the universe does (so irrelevant tuples must be excluded with NOT R(x)R(x)R(x) OR …); each can be rewritten with the other plus negation.

    What the grader checks

    Truth conditions of both, the “exclude other tuples” idiom for ∀\forall∀, the transformation rule, and an example of each (“some” vs. “all”).

    8.11TRC termsE&N Ex. 8.11 · p. 281

    Define the following terms with respect to the tuple calculus: tuple variable, range relation, atom, formula, and expression.

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Tuple variable: a variable whose values are tuples (ttt, ddd, eee); t.At.At.A is the value of attribute AAA in ttt.
    • Range relation: the relation over which a tuple variable ranges, stated by the atom R(t)R(t)R(t) (EMPLOYEE(t)\textsf{EMPLOYEE}(t)EMPLOYEE(t)); without it ttt ranges over all tuples in the universe.
    • Atom: one of R(ti)R(t_i)R(ti​); ti.A op tj.Bt_i.A\ \text{op}\ t_j.Bti​.A op tj​.B; ti.A op ct_i.A\ \text{op}\ cti​.A op c (or c op tj.Bc\ \text{op}\ t_j.Bc op tj​.B), op ∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\ne\}∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=}. It evaluates to TRUE or FALSE for an assignment of tuples.
    • Formula (WFF): built recursively: every atom is a formula; if F1,F2F_1,F_2F1​,F2​ are formulas so are (F1andF2)(F_1\mathbin{\textbf{and}} F_2)(F1​andF2​), (F1orF2)(F_1\mathbin{\textbf{or}} F_2)(F1​orF2​), not (F1)\textbf{not}\, (F_1)not(F1​), (∃t)(F)(\exists t)(F)(∃t)(F), (∀t)(F)(\forall t)(F)(∀t)(F).
    • Expression: {t1.Aj,t2.Ak,…,tn.Am∣COND(t1,…,tn+m)}\{t_1.A_j, t_2.A_k,\dots,t_n.A_m\mid\text{COND}(t_1,\dots,t_{n+m})\}{t1​.Aj​,t2​.Ak​,…,tn​.Am​∣COND(t1​,…,tn+m​)}: the requested attributes of the free variables for every assignment that makes the formula TRUE; e.g. {t.Fname,t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000}\{t.\text{Fname}, t.\text{Lname}\mid \textsf{EMPLOYEE}(t)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\text{Salary}>50000\}{t.Fname,t.Lname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Salary>50000} = James Borg.
    8.12DRC termsE&N Ex. 8.12 · p. 281

    Define the following terms with respect to the domain calculus: domain variable, range relation, atom, formula, and expression.

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Domain variable: a variable ranging over the values of an attribute domain (q,r,…,zq,r,\dots,zq,r,…,z for EMPLOYEE’s ten attributes).
    • Range relation: given by an atom R(x1x2…xj)R(x_1x_2\dots x_j)R(x1​x2​…xj​), which says the list of values is a tuple of RRR (the iii-th variable takes the iii-th attribute’s value).
    • Atom: R(x1…xj)R(x_1\dots x_j)R(x1​…xj​); xi op xjx_i\ \text{op}\ x_jxi​ op xj​; xi op cx_i\ \text{op}\ cxi​ op c (or c op xjc\ \text{op}\ x_jc op xj​), op ∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,≠}\in\{=,<,\le,>,\ge,\ne\}∈{=,<,≤,>,≥,=}.
    • Formula: atoms combined with AND, OR, NOT and quantifiers (∃x)(\exists x)(∃x), (∀x)(\forall x)(∀x), exactly as in TRC.
    • Expression: {x1,…,xn∣COND(x1,…,xn,xn+1,…,xn+m)}\{x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\text{COND}(x_1,\dots,x_n,x_{n+1},\dots,x_{n+m})\}{x1​,…,xn​∣COND(x1​,…,xn​,xn+1​,…,xn+m​)}, with nnn free variables, one per result attribute. Example (Q0): {u,v∣(∃q)(∃r)(∃s)(EMPLOYEE(qrstuvwxyz)andq=‘John’andr=‘B’ands=‘Smith’)}\{u,v\mid(\exists q)(\exists r)(\exists s)(\textsf{EMPLOYEE}(qrstuvwxyz)\mathbin{\textbf{and}} q=\text{`John'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}} r=\text{`B'}\mathbin{\textbf{and}} s=\text{`Smith'})\}{u,v∣(∃q)(∃r)(∃s)(EMPLOYEE(qrstuvwxyz)andq=‘John’andr=‘B’ands=‘Smith’)} gives Smith’s birth date and address.

    Textbook exercises

    Conventions used in every solution below
    • Relations are sets: π\piπ removes duplicate tuples. Every query is built from named intermediate relations (X←EX \leftarrow EX←E); the last one is the answer. Base relations are in sans-serif (EMPLOYEE), temporaries in italics (PX\mathit{PX}PX).
    • ⋈c\bowtie_c⋈c​ is a theta join, ∗*∗ the natural join (equates all same-named attributes), ÷\div÷ division, ρR(A1,… )\rho_{R(A_1,\dots)}ρR(A1​,…)​ renaming, ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕/⟖\mathbin{\text{⟖}}⟖/⟗\mathbin{\text{⟗}}⟗ left/right/full outer join.
    • G IF A(R){}_{\text{G}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{F A}}\left(R\right)G​IF A​(R) groups RRR on GGG and applies FFF to AAA over the tuples of each group (no grouping attributes = one tuple for the whole relation). SUM/AVERAGE/MIN/MAX ignore NULLs; COUNT AAA counts the non-NULL AAA values. A comparison with NULL is never true, so σ\sigmaσ and ⋈\bowtie⋈ drop such tuples.
    • The two Moodle RA keys (RA-I, RA-G) award marks for: stated, justified assumptions; the correct join condition for every join; the “all”/“no” condition done by difference or division; the exact output attributes.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Keys and foreign keys are those of Figure 5.5: Super_ssn, Mgr_ssn, WORKS_ON.Essn, DEPENDENT.Essn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn; Dno, Dnum, DEPT_LOCATIONS.Dnumber → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber; Pno → PROJECT.Pnumber. Why: the book’s schema (Fig. 5.7) states these, and they decide every join condition below.
    2. A “name” is (Fname, Lname). Why: the question does not ask for Minit. Two different employees with the same name would show as one row; adding Ssn to the output avoids this and is equally acceptable.
    3. “Works on a project” means having a WORKS_ON tuple for it, even if Hours is NULL (Borg on project 20). Why: the tuple records the assignment; NULL means the hours are unknown.
    4. Aggregates ignore NULLs (Borg’s NULL hours add nothing to project 20’s total). Why: these are the standard SUM/AVERAGE semantics, as in SQL.
    5. (e) “every project” means every project in PROJECT, whichever department controls it. Why: the question puts no restriction on the projects.

    (a) Department-5 employees with more than 10 hours on ProductX

    What the grader checks
    • Join conditions. EMPLOYEE∗WORKS_ON\textsf{EMPLOYEE}\mathbin{*}\textsf{WORKS\_ON}EMPLOYEE∗WORKS_ON has no common attribute, so it is a Cartesian product: 0 for that criterion. Write ⋈Ssn=Essn\bowtie_{\text{Ssn=Essn}}⋈Ssn=Essn​, or rename first. A ×\times× without a following selection is the same mistake.
    • “Every” (e) needs ÷\div÷, or the double difference. Projecting away Hours before ÷\div÷ is part of the answer. “No/not any” (f, i, j) needs a set difference; a selection with ≠\neq= is existential and loses the marks.
    • Union compatibility. −-− and ∩\cap∩ need the same number of attributes over the same domains. Project both sides to the Ssn first; EMPLOYEE−WORKS_ON\textsf{EMPLOYEE} - \textsf{WORKS\_ON}EMPLOYEE−WORKS_ON is undefined, which gives 0.
    • Aggregation: group on the key (Pno, Dno), not the name. Never project before SUM/AVERAGE (pitfall above).
    • Output: exactly the attributes asked for (names, last names only in (j), names and addresses in (i)).

    Verified: every query was run step by step with a Python RA evaluator on the Figure 5.6 instance and cross-checked against equivalent SQL in sqlite3. All ten results match.

    8.17AIRLINE queriesE&N Ex. 8.17 · p. 282

    Consider the AIRLINE relational database schema shown in Figure 5.8, which was described in Exercise 5.12. Specify the following queries in relational algebra:

    1. For each flight, list the flight number, the departure airport for the first leg of the flight, and the arrival airport for the last leg of the flight.
    2. List the flight numbers and weekdays of all flights or flight legs that depart from Houston Intercontinental Airport (airport code ‘iah’) and arrive in Los Angeles International Airport (airport code ‘lax’).
    3. List the flight number, departure airport code, scheduled departure time, arrival airport code, scheduled arrival time, and weekdays of all flights or flight legs that depart from some airport in the city of Houston and arrive at some airport in the city of Los Angeles.
    4. List all fare information for flight number ‘co197’.
    5. Retrieve the number of available seats for flight number ‘co197’ on ‘2009-10-09’.

    Schema (Figure 5.8). AIRPORT(Airport_code, Name, City, State); FLIGHT(Flight_number, Airline, Weekdays); FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time); LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Number_of_available_seats, Airplane_id, Departure_airport_code, Departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Arrival_time); FARE(Flight_number, Fare_code, Amount, Restrictions); AIRPLANE_TYPE(Airplane_type_name, Max_seats, Company); CAN_LAND(Airplane_type_name, Airport_code); AIRPLANE(Airplane_id, Total_number_of_seats, Airplane_type); SEAT_RESERVATION(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number, Customer_name, Customer_phone).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Leg order. The legs of a flight are numbered in flying order, so the first leg has the smallest Leg_number and the last leg the largest. Why: nothing else in the schema orders legs. Using MIN/MAX does not assume that numbering starts at 1.
    2. “Flights or flight legs” (b, c). A flight qualifies either if one of its legs goes from the origin to the destination, or if the whole flight does (first leg departs from the origin, last leg arrives at the destination). Why: the question says “flights or flight legs”. Answering only the leg reading is also common, if it is stated.
    3. Cities. The city names stored in AIRPORT are ‘Houston’ and ‘Los Angeles’. Why: part (c) asks for any airport in the city, so the codes must come from AIRPORT, not be hard-coded.
    4. (e) Available seats are stored per leg per date in LEG_INSTANCE. The answer lists them per leg. The number available for the whole flight is the minimum over its legs (a through passenger needs a seat on every leg). Why: the schema has no flight-level seat count.

    (a) First-leg departure and last-leg arrival of each flight

    G←Flight_number IMIN Leg_number, MAX Leg_number(FLIGHT_LEG)FL_LEGS←ρFL_LEGS(Flight_number, First_leg, Last_leg)(G)F0←πFlight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time(FLIGHT_LEG)FIRST←ρFIRST(Flight_number, First_leg, Dep_code, Dep_time)(F0)L0←πFlight_number, Leg_number, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time(FLIGHT_LEG)LAST←ρLAST(Flight_number, Last_leg, Arr_code, Arr_time)(L0)FL←FL_LEGS∗FIRST∗LASTRESULT←πFlight_number, Dep_code, Arr_code(FL)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{G} &\leftarrow& {}_{\text{Flight\_number}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{MIN Leg\_number, MAX Leg\_number}}\left(\textsf{FLIGHT\_LEG}\right) \\ \mathit{FL\_LEGS} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{FL\_LEGS(Flight\_number, First\_leg, Last\_leg)}}\left(\mathit{G}\right) \\ \mathit{F0} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Flight\_number, Leg\_number, Departure\_airport\_code, Scheduled\_departure\_time}}\left(\textsf{FLIGHT\_LEG}\right) \\ \mathit{FIRST} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{FIRST(Flight\_number, First\_leg, Dep\_code, Dep\_time)}}\left(\mathit{F0}\right) \\ \mathit{L0} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Flight\_number, Leg\_number, Arrival\_airport\_code, Scheduled\_arrival\_time}}\left(\textsf{FLIGHT\_LEG}\right) \\ \mathit{LAST} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{LAST(Flight\_number, Last\_leg, Arr\_code, Arr\_time)}}\left(\mathit{L0}\right) \\ \mathit{FL} &\leftarrow& \mathit{FL\_LEGS} \mathbin{*} \mathit{FIRST} \mathbin{*} \mathit{LAST} \\ Arr\_code}}\left(\mathit{FL}\right)\end{array}GFL_LEGSF0FIRSTL0LASTFLRESULT​←←←←←←←←​Flight_number​IMIN Leg_number, MAX Leg_number​(FLIGHT_LEG)ρFL_LEGS(Flight_number, First_leg, Last_leg)​(G)πFlight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time​(FLIGHT_LEG)ρFIRST(Flight_number, First_leg, Dep_code, Dep_time)​(F0)πFlight_number, Leg_number, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time​(FLIGHT_LEG)ρLAST(Flight_number, Last_leg, Arr_code, Arr_time)​(L0)FL_LEGS∗FIRST∗LASTπFlight_number, Dep_code, Arr_code​(FL)​

    FL_LEGS\mathit{FL\_LEGS}FL_LEGS finds the first and last leg numbers of each flight. FIRST\mathit{FIRST}FIRST and LAST\mathit{LAST}LAST are two renamed copies of FLIGHT_LEG. Renaming Leg_number to First_leg (resp. Last_leg) makes the natural joins match on (Flight_number, First_leg) and (Flight_number, Last_leg), so they pick exactly the first and the last leg. FL\mathit{FL}FL also keeps the times, which (c) reuses.

    (b) Flights/legs from ‘iah’ to ‘lax’

    LEGB←πFlight_number(σDeparture_airport_code = ‘iah’ ∧ Arrival_airport_code = ‘lax’(FLIGHT_LEG))FLB←πFlight_number(σDep_code = ‘iah’ ∧ Arr_code = ‘lax’(FL))RESULT←πFlight_number, Weekdays((LEGB∪FLB)∗FLIGHT)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{LEGB} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Flight\_number}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Departure\_airport\_code = `iah' $\wedge$ Arrival\_airport\_code = `lax'}}\left(\textsf{FLIGHT\_LEG}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{FLB} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Flight\_number}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Dep\_code = `iah' $\wedge$ Arr\_code = `lax'}}\left(\mathit{FL}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Flight\_number, Weekdays}}\left((\mathit{LEGB} \cup \mathit{FLB}) \mathbin{*} \textsf{FLIGHT}\right)\end{array}LEGBFLBRESULT​←←←​πFlight_number​(σDeparture_airport_code = ‘iah’ ∧ Arrival_airport_code = ‘lax’​(FLIGHT_LEG))πFlight_number​(σDep_code = ‘iah’ ∧ Arr_code = ‘lax’​(FL))πFlight_number, Weekdays​((LEGB∪FLB)∗FLIGHT)​

    LEGB\mathit{LEGB}LEGB is the leg reading and FLB\mathit{FLB}FLB the whole-flight reading (A2). Both are {Flight_number}, so ∪\cup∪ is defined. Weekdays is an attribute of FLIGHT, so the last step joins it in.

    (c) Flights/legs from any Houston airport to any Los Angeles airport

&\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{HOU(Hcode)}}\left(\pi_{\text{Airport\_code}}\left(\sigma_{\text{City = `Houston'}}\left(\textsf{AIRPORT}\right)\right)\right) \\ \mathit{LA} &\leftarrow& Scheduled\_arrival\_time}\end{subarray}}\left(\textsf{FLIGHT\_LEG}\right) \\ \mathit{LEG5} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{LEG5(Flight\_number, Dep\_code, Dep\_time, Arr\_code, Arr\_time)}}\left(\mathit{LG0}\right) \\ \mathit{LEGC} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{$\mathcal{A}$}}\left((\mathit{LEG5} \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Dep\_code = Hcode}}} \mathit{HOU})
