\mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Arr\_code = Lcode}}} \mathit{LA}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{$\mathcal{A}$, Weekdays}}\left((\mathit{LEGC} \cup \mathit{FLC}) \mathbin{*} \textsf{FLIGHT}\right)\end{array}HOULALG0LEG5LEGCFLCRESULT​←←←←←←←​ρHOU(Hcode)​(πAirport_code​(σCity = ‘Houston’​(AIRPORT)))ρLA(Lcode)​(πAirport_code​(σCity = ‘Los Angeles’​(AIRPORT)))πFlight_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time,Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time​​(FLIGHT_LEG)ρLEG5(Flight_number, Dep_code, Dep_time, Arr_code, Arr_time)​(LG0)πA​((LEG5⋈Dep_code = Hcode​HOU)⋈Arr_code = Lcode​LA)πA​((FL⋈Dep_code = Hcode​HOU)⋈Arr_code = Lcode​LA)πA, Weekdays​((LEGC∪FLC)∗FLIGHT)​

    Here A\mathcal{A}A abbreviates (Flight_number, Dep_code, Dep_time, Arr_code, Arr_time). HOU\mathit{HOU}HOU and LA\mathit{LA}LA hold all the airport codes in each city. LEG5\mathit{LEG5}LEG5 gives the leg attributes the same names that FL\mathit{FL}FL uses, so that LEGC\mathit{LEGC}LEGC and FLC\mathit{FLC}FLC are union-compatible. For a whole flight the times reported are the first leg’s departure and the last leg’s arrival.

    (d) Fares of co197

    RESULT←σFlight_number = ‘co197’(FARE)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Flight\_number = `co197'}}\left(\textsf{FARE}\right)\end{array}RESULT​←​σFlight_number = ‘co197’​(FARE)​

    “All fare information” means all attributes of FARE, so no projection is needed.

    (e) Available seats on co197 on 2009-10-09

    LI←σFlight_number = ‘co197’ ∧ Date = ‘2009-10-09’(LEG_INSTANCE)RESULT←πLeg_number, Number_of_available_seats(LI)WHOLE←ρWHOLE(Seats)( IMIN Number_of_available_seats(LI))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{LI} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Flight\_number = `co197' $\wedge$ Date = `2009-10-09'}}\left(\textsf{LEG\_INSTANCE}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Leg\_number, Number\_of\_available\_seats}}\left(\mathit{LI}\right) \\ \mathit{WHOLE} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{WHOLE(Seats)}}\left({}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{MIN Number\_of\_available\_seats}}\left(\mathit{LI}\right)\right)\end{array}LIRESULTWHOLE​←←←​σFlight_number = ‘co197’ ∧ Date = ‘2009-10-09’​(LEG_INSTANCE)πLeg_number, Number_of_available_seats​(LI)ρWHOLE(Seats)​(​IMIN Number_of_available_seats​(LI))​

    RESULT\mathit{RESULT}RESULT gives the seats per leg. WHOLE\mathit{WHOLE}WHOLE gives the seats available to someone flying the whole flight (A4). Leg_number must stay in the projection, or two legs with equal seat counts would merge.

    Answer

    The RESULT\mathit{RESULT}RESULT relations above. Use γ\gammaγ MIN/MAX of Leg_number to find the end legs, and join them back through renamed copies of FLIGHT_LEG.

    What the grader checks
    • (a) “First/last leg” needs an aggregate (or Leg_number=1 together with a stated assumption for the first leg). The last leg cannot be found by a selection on a constant. Joining the MIN and MAX rows through one un-renamed copy of FLIGHT_LEG equates Leg_number with both, which is wrong.
    • (c) Hard-coding ‘iah’/‘lax’ loses the “some airport in the city” condition. Get the codes from AIRPORT.
    • Weekdays comes from FLIGHT, so the join must be on Flight_number. Both operands of ∪\cup∪ must have the same attribute list.

    Verified with the Python RA evaluator on a test instance that contains a direct iah→\to→lax flight, a 2-leg iah→\to→dfw→\to→lax flight (whole-flight match only), a lax→\to→iah→\to→lax flight (leg match only), a Hobby (Houston)→\to→Burbank (LA) flight (matches (c) only) and a dfw→\to→iah flight (no match). Each flight appeared in exactly the right parts.

    8.18LIBRARY queriesE&N Ex. 8.18 · p. 282★ Must-do

    Consider the LIBRARY relational database schema shown in Figure 8.14, which is used to keep track of books, borrowers, and book loans. Referential integrity constraints are shown as directed arcs in Figure 8.14, as in the notation of Figure 5.7. Write down relational expressions for the following queries:

    1. How many copies of the book titled The Lost Tribe are owned by the library branch whose name is ‘Sharpstown’?
    2. How many copies of the book titled The Lost Tribe are owned by each library branch?
    3. Retrieve the names of all borrowers who do not have any books checked out.
    4. For each book that is loaned out from the Sharpstown branch and whose Due_date is today, retrieve the book title, the borrower’s name, and the borrower’s address.
    5. For each library branch, retrieve the branch name and the total number of books loaned out from that branch.
    6. Retrieve the names, addresses, and number of books checked out for all borrowers who have more than five books checked out.
    7. For each book authored (or coauthored) by Stephen King, retrieve the title and the number of copies owned by the library branch whose name is Central.

    Schema (Figure 8.14). BOOK(Book_id, Title, Publisher_name); BOOK_AUTHORS(Book_id, Author_name); PUBLISHER(Name, Address, Phone); BOOK_COPIES(Book_id, Branch_id, No_of_copies); BOOK_LOANS(Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no, Date_out, Due_date); LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id, Branch_name, Address); BORROWER(Card_no, Name, Address, Phone). FKs (arcs): Book_id in BOOK_AUTHORS, BOOK_COPIES and BOOK_LOANS → BOOK; Publisher_name → PUBLISHER.Name; Branch_id in BOOK_COPIES and BOOK_LOANS → LIBRARY_BRANCH; BOOK_LOANS.Card_no → BORROWER.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Branch names and the title are identifying. Exactly one branch is named ‘Sharpstown’ (and one ‘Central’), and one book is titled The Lost Tribe. Why: the question says “the library branch” and “the book”. If there were several, the SUM used in (a) would total them.
    2. A BOOK_LOANS tuple is one copy currently checked out. Why: the relation has no return date, so a returned loan must have been deleted. Its key (Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no) means that “number of books” is the number of loan tuples.
    3. “Today” is a constant TODAY (the current date when the query runs). Why: RA has no clock.
    4. Address clash. BORROWER, LIBRARY_BRANCH and PUBLISHER all have an Address (and two have Phone). They mean different things, so every join below projects them away first, to stop a natural join from equating them.

    (a) Copies of The Lost Tribe at Sharpstown

    LT←πBook_id(σTitle = ‘The Lost Tribe’(BOOK))SH←πBranch_id(σBranch_name = ‘Sharpstown’(LIBRARY_BRANCH))RESULT←ρRESULT(Copies)( ISUM No_of_copies(BOOK_COPIES∗LT∗SH))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{LT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Book\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Title = `The Lost Tribe'}}\left(\textsf{BOOK}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{SH} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Branch\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Branch\_name = `Sharpstown'}}\left(\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{RESULT(Copies)}}\left({}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM No\_of\_copies}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_COPIES} \mathbin{*} \mathit{LT} \mathbin{*} \mathit{SH}\right)\right)\end{array}LTSHRESULT​←←←​πBook_id​(σTitle = ‘The Lost Tribe’​(BOOK))πBranch_id​(σBranch_name = ‘Sharpstown’​(LIBRARY_BRANCH))ρRESULT(Copies)​(​ISUM No_of_copies​(BOOK_COPIES∗LT∗SH))​

    The natural joins match on Book_id and Branch_id, which leaves the single BOOK_COPIES tuple for that book and branch. Under A1, πNo_of_copies(⋯ )\pi_{\text{No\_of\_copies}}\left(\cdots\right)πNo_of_copies​(⋯) gives the same answer. If the branch owns no copies, the SUM is NULL (no tuple), which means 0.

    (b) Copies of The Lost Tribe per branch

    LTC←BOOK_COPIES∗LTRESULT←Branch_id, Branch_name ISUM No_of_copies(LTC∗πBranch_id, Branch_name(LIBRARY_BRANCH))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{LTC} &\leftarrow& \textsf{BOOK\_COPIES} \mathbin{*} \mathit{LT} \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& {}_{\text{Branch\_id, Branch\_name}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM No\_of\_copies}}\left(\mathit{LTC} \mathbin{*} \pi_{\text{Branch\_id, Branch\_name}}\left(\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\right)\right)\end{array}LTCRESULT​←←​BOOK_COPIES∗LTBranch_id, Branch_name​ISUM No_of_copies​(LTC∗πBranch_id, Branch_name​(LIBRARY_BRANCH))​

    Grouping on Branch_id (the key) keeps branches with the same name apart; Branch_name is kept for display. Branches with no copies do not appear. To list them with NULL, use πBranch_id, Branch_name(LIBRARY_BRANCH)⟕LTC\pi_{\text{Branch\_id, Branch\_name}}\left(\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\right) \mathbin{\text{⟕}} \mathit{LTC}πBranch_id, Branch_name​(LIBRARY_BRANCH)⟕LTC.

    (c) Borrowers with nothing checked out

    NONE←πCard_no(BORROWER)−πCard_no(BOOK_LOANS)RESULT←πName(NONE∗BORROWER)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{NONE} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Card\_no}}\left(\textsf{BORROWER}\right) - \pi_{\text{Card\_no}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Name}}\left(\mathit{NONE} \mathbin{*} \textsf{BORROWER}\right)\end{array}NONERESULT​←←​πCard_no​(BORROWER)−πCard_no​(BOOK_LOANS)πName​(NONE∗BORROWER)​

    Both sides of −-− are {Card_no}, so they are union-compatible. The difference is computed on the key, not on Name: two borrowers with the same name must not cancel each other.

    (d) Sharpstown loans due today: title, borrower name and address

    DL←σDue_date = TODAY(BOOK_LOANS∗SH)DLB←DL∗πBook_id, Title(BOOK)RESULT←πTitle, Name, Address(DLB∗πCard_no, Name, Address(BORROWER))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{DL} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Due\_date = \textit{TODAY}}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS} \mathbin{*} \mathit{SH}\right) \\ \mathit{DLB} &\leftarrow& \mathit{DL} \mathbin{*} \pi_{\text{Book\_id, Title}}\left(\textsf{BOOK}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Title, Name, Address}}\left(\mathit{DLB} \mathbin{*} \pi_{\text{Card\_no, Name, Address}}\left(\textsf{BORROWER}\right)\right)\end{array}DLDLBRESULT​←←←​σDue_date = TODAY​(BOOK_LOANS∗SH)DL∗πBook_id, Title​(BOOK)πTitle, Name, Address​(DLB∗πCard_no, Name, Address​(BORROWER))​

    DL\mathit{DL}DL is the loans from Sharpstown (SH\mathit{SH}SH from (a)) that are due today. The join with SH\mathit{SH}SH contributes only Branch_id, so the branch’s Address never enters. DLB\mathit{DLB}DLB adds the title, and the last join adds the borrower’s Name and Address. Every Address here is the borrower’s.

    (e) Number of books on loan per branch

    LC←ρLC(Branch_id, Num_loans)(Branch_id ICOUNT Book_id(BOOK_LOANS))RESULT←πBranch_name, Num_loans(πBranch_id, Branch_name(LIBRARY_BRANCH)∗LC)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{LC} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{LC(Branch\_id, Num\_loans)}}\left({}_{\text{Branch\_id}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Book\_id}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Branch\_name, Num\_loans}}\left(\pi_{\text{Branch\_id, Branch\_name}}\left(\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\right) \mathbin{*} \mathit{LC}\right)\end{array}LCRESULT​←←​ρLC(Branch_id, Num_loans)​(Branch_id​ICOUNT Book_id​(BOOK_LOANS))πBranch_name, Num_loans​(πBranch_id, Branch_name​(LIBRARY_BRANCH)∗LC)​

    Each loan tuple is one book on loan (A2), so the count runs over the tuples of BOOK_LOANS. Branches with no loans are missing; using ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕ in the last step would list them with NULL.

    (f) Borrowers with more than five books out

    BC←ρBC(Card_no, Num_out)(Card_no ICOUNT Book_id(BOOK_LOANS))MANY←σNum_out > 5(BC)RESULT←πName, Address, Num_out(MANY∗BORROWER)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{BC} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{BC(Card\_no, Num\_out)}}\left({}_{\text{Card\_no}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Book\_id}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{MANY} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Num\_out $>$ 5}}\left(\mathit{BC}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Name, Address, Num\_out}}\left(\mathit{MANY} \mathbin{*} \textsf{BORROWER}\right)\end{array}BCMANYRESULT​←←←​ρBC(Card_no, Num_out)​(Card_no​ICOUNT Book_id​(BOOK_LOANS))σNum_out > 5​(BC)πName, Address, Num_out​(MANY∗BORROWER)​

    The selection on the aggregate comes after the grouping, like SQL’s HAVING.

    Counting after a projection

    Card_no ICOUNT Book_id(πCard_no, Book_id(BOOK_LOANS)){}_{\text{Card\_no}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Book\_id}}\left(\pi_{\text{Card\_no, Book\_id}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS}\right)\right)Card_no​ICOUNT Book_id​(πCard_no, Book_id​(BOOK_LOANS)) undercounts. A borrower with the same title from two branches has two loan tuples but only one (Card_no, Book_id) pair. In the test instance this gave 4 instead of 6, so the borrower was wrongly excluded.

    (g) Stephen King books: title and copies at Central

    SK←πBook_id(σAuthor_name = ‘Stephen King’(BOOK_AUTHORS))SKB←πBook_id, Title(SK∗BOOK)CEN←πBook_id, No_of_copies(BOOK_COPIES∗πBranch_id(σBranch_name = ‘Central’(LIBRARY_BRANCH)))RESULT←πTitle, No_of_copies(SKB⟕CEN)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{SK} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Book\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Author\_name = `Stephen King'}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_AUTHORS}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{SKB} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Book\_id, Title}}\left(\mathit{SK} \mathbin{*} \textsf{BOOK}\right) \\ \mathit{CEN} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Book\_id, No\_of\_copies}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_COPIES} \mathbin{*} \pi_{\text{Branch\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Branch\_name = `Central'}}\left(\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\right)\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Title, No\_of\_copies}}\left(\mathit{SKB} \mathbin{\text{⟕}} \mathit{CEN}\right)\end{array}SKSKBCENRESULT​←←←←​πBook_id​(σAuthor_name = ‘Stephen King’​(BOOK_AUTHORS))πBook_id, Title​(SK∗BOOK)πBook_id, No_of_copies​(BOOK_COPIES∗πBranch_id​(σBranch_name = ‘Central’​(LIBRARY_BRANCH)))πTitle, No_of_copies​(SKB⟕CEN)​

    BOOK_AUTHORS lists every author of a book, so SK\mathit{SK}SK covers both sole-authored and coauthored books. The left outer join keeps King books that Central does not own (with NULL copies, which means 0). With an inner join they disappear, which is acceptable only if stated. Keep Book_id in the output if two King books might share a title.

    Answer

    The RESULT\mathit{RESULT}RESULT relations above. The key moves: −-− on Card_no for (c); grouping on the key with COUNT/SUM, and selection on the aggregate after it, for (b), (e), (f); projecting away the clashing Address attributes before natural joins in (d).

    What the grader checks
    • (d): BOOK_LOANS∗LIBRARY_BRANCH∗BOOK∗BORROWER\textsf{BOOK\_LOANS}\mathbin{*}\textsf{LIBRARY\_BRANCH}\mathbin{*}\textsf{BOOK}\mathbin{*}\textsf{BORROWER}BOOK_LOANS∗LIBRARY_BRANCH∗BOOK∗BORROWER also equates the branch’s Address with the borrower’s. That keeps only loans whose borrower lives at the branch’s address (1 of the 8 loans in the test instance). This is a wrong join condition.
    • (c): a selection such as σCard_no≠…\sigma_{\text{Card\_no}\neq\ldots}σCard_no=…​ cannot express “no loans”; use −-−.
    • (e), (f): group on the key (Branch_id, Card_no), not the name, and count loan tuples. “More than five” is >5>5>5, not ≥5\geq 5≥5.
    • (a), (b), (g): the title and branch name are selected, then joined through the keys; a ×\times× with no join condition loses the marks.

    Verified with the Python RA evaluator on a test LIBRARY instance (3 branches, one with no copies; a borrower with 6 loans, including the same book from two branches; a borrower with none; a borrower living at a branch address; a coauthored King book; a King book not at Central). The expected rows came out, and the wrong variants above behaved as described.

    8.19Order-processing queries (schema of Exercise 5.14)E&N Ex. 8.19 · p. 282

    Specify the following queries in relational algebra on the database schema given in Exercise 5.14: CUSTOMER(Cust#, Cname, City); ORDER(Order#, Odate, Cust#, Ord_amt); ORDER_ITEM(Order#, Item#, Qty); ITEM(Item#, Unit_price); SHIPMENT(Order#, Warehouse#, Ship_date); WAREHOUSE(Warehouse#, City). (Ord_amt is the total dollar amount of an order; Odate is the date the order was placed; Ship_date is the date an order, or part of an order, is shipped from the warehouse. An order can be shipped from several warehouses.)

    1. List the Order# and Ship_date for all orders shipped from Warehouse# W2.
    2. List the WAREHOUSE information from which the CUSTOMER named Jose Lopez was supplied his orders. Produce a listing: Order#, Warehouse#.
    3. Produce a listing Cname, No_of_orders, Avg_order_amt, where the middle column is the total number of orders by the customer and the last column is the average order amount for that customer.
    4. List the orders that were not shipped within 30 days of ordering.
    5. List the Order# for orders that were shipped from all warehouses that the company has in New York.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. FKs: ORDER.Cust# → CUSTOMER, SHIPMENT.Order# → ORDER, SHIPMENT.Warehouse# → WAREHOUSE, and ORDER_ITEM references ORDER and ITEM. Why: these are the answers to Exercise 5.14; they make every natural join below match on exactly one attribute. CUSTOMER and WAREHOUSE both have City, so they are never natural-joined together.
    2. Dates can be subtracted, giving a number of days. Why: needed for (d); this is the standard date arithmetic of SQL/RA texts.
    3. (d) An order is “not shipped within 30 days” if some shipment of it has Ship_date−Odate>30\textsf{Ship\_date} - \textsf{Odate} > 30Ship_date−Odate>30. Why: an order shipped in parts is complete only when its last part ships. Orders with no shipment at all are not “shipped”, so they are not listed (they could be added by a difference with ORDER if the reading “not yet shipped” is wanted).
    4. (e) “All” over an empty set. If the company has no New York warehouse, every shipped order qualifies vacuously (“for all” over an empty set is true). Why: this is what ÷\div÷ computes, and it agrees with the RA-I key’s convention (A5 there).
    5. (b) There may be several customers named Jose Lopez; the query covers all of them. Why: Cname is not a key.

    (a) Orders shipped from W2

    RESULT←πOrder#, Ship_date(σWarehouse# = ‘W2’(SHIPMENT))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Order\#, Ship\_date}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Warehouse\# = `W2'}}\left(\textsf{SHIPMENT}\right)\right)\end{array}RESULT​←​πOrder#, Ship_date​(σWarehouse# = ‘W2’​(SHIPMENT))​

    SHIPMENT holds one tuple per (order, warehouse), so this is a single selection and projection.

    (b) Order#, Warehouse# for Jose Lopez’s orders

    JL←πCust#(σCname = ‘Jose Lopez’(CUSTOMER))JLO←πOrder#(JL∗ORDER)RESULT←πOrder#, Warehouse#(JLO∗SHIPMENT)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{JL} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Cust\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Cname = `Jose Lopez'}}\left(\textsf{CUSTOMER}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{JLO} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Order\#}}\left(\mathit{JL} \mathbin{*} \textsf{ORDER}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Order\#, Warehouse\#}}\left(\mathit{JLO} \mathbin{*} \textsf{SHIPMENT}\right)\end{array}JLJLORESULT​←←←​πCust#​(σCname = ‘Jose Lopez’​(CUSTOMER))πOrder#​(JL∗ORDER)πOrder#, Warehouse#​(JLO∗SHIPMENT)​

    The customer’s City is projected away in JL\mathit{JL}JL. The chain is customer →\to→ orders (on Cust#) →\to→ shipments (on Order#).

    (c) Cname, number of orders, average order amount

    CO←ρCO(Cust#, No_of_orders, Avg_order_amt)(Cust# ICOUNT Order#, AVERAGE Ord_amt(ORDER))RESULT←πCname, No_of_orders, Avg_order_amt(CUSTOMER∗CO)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{CO} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{CO(Cust\#, No\_of\_orders, Avg\_order\_amt)}}\left({}_{\text{Cust\#}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Order\#, AVERAGE Ord\_amt}}\left(\textsf{ORDER}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Cname, No\_of\_orders, Avg\_order\_amt}}\left(\textsf{CUSTOMER} \mathbin{*} \mathit{CO}\right)\end{array}CORESULT​←←​ρCO(Cust#, No_of_orders, Avg_order_amt)​(Cust#​ICOUNT Order#, AVERAGE Ord_amt​(ORDER))πCname, No_of_orders, Avg_order_amt​(CUSTOMER∗CO)​

    Grouping is on Cust#, so two customers who are both named Jose Lopez get separate rows. Both aggregates run over the whole ORDER relation (no projection first). Customers with no orders are omitted; using CUSTOMER⟕CO\textsf{CUSTOMER}\mathbin{\text{⟕}}\mathit{CO}CUSTOMER⟕CO would keep them with NULLs.

    (d) Orders not shipped within 30 days

    OS←ORDER∗SHIPMENTRESULT←πOrder#(σShip_date − Odate > 30(OS))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{OS} &\leftarrow& \textsf{ORDER} \mathbin{*} \textsf{SHIPMENT} \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Order\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Ship\_date $-$ Odate $>$ 30}}\left(\mathit{OS}\right)\right)\end{array}OSRESULT​←←​ORDER∗SHIPMENTπOrder#​(σShip_date − Odate > 30​(OS))​

    The natural join pairs each order with each of its shipments, on Order#. The selection keeps late shipments (A3). The question asks to “list the orders”, so Order# identifies them; RESULT∗ORDER\mathit{RESULT}\mathbin{*}\textsf{ORDER}RESULT∗ORDER would give full rows.

    (e) Orders shipped from every New York warehouse (division)

    NY←πWarehouse#(σCity = ‘New York’(WAREHOUSE))OW←πOrder#, Warehouse#(SHIPMENT)RESULT←OW÷NY\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{NY} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Warehouse\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{City = `New York'}}\left(\textsf{WAREHOUSE}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{OW} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Order\#, Warehouse\#}}\left(\textsf{SHIPMENT}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \mathit{OW} \mathbin{\div} \mathit{NY}\end{array}NYOWRESULT​←←←​πWarehouse#​(σCity = ‘New York’​(WAREHOUSE))πOrder#, Warehouse#​(SHIPMENT)OW÷NY​

    OW\mathit{OW}OW must drop Ship_date. Otherwise the quotient would be (Order#, Ship_date) and an order shipped from two NY warehouses on different dates would fail. By A4, if NY\mathit{NY}NY is empty, OW÷NY=πOrder#(OW)\mathit{OW}\div \mathit{NY}=\pi_{\text{Order\#}}\left(\mathit{OW}\right)OW÷NY=πOrder#​(OW).

    Answer

    (a) π\piπ/σ\sigmaσ on SHIPMENT. (b) CUSTOMER→\to→ORDER→\to→SHIPMENT via the keys. (c) γ\gammaγ on Cust# with COUNT and AVERAGE. (d) σ\sigmaσ on the date difference after joining ORDER and SHIPMENT. (e) πOrder#, Warehouse#(SHIPMENT)÷πWarehouse#(σCity=‘New York’(WAREHOUSE))\pi_{\text{Order\#, Warehouse\#}}\left(\textsf{SHIPMENT}\right) \div \pi_{\text{Warehouse\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{City=`New York'}}\left(\textsf{WAREHOUSE}\right)\right)πOrder#, Warehouse#​(SHIPMENT)÷πWarehouse#​(σCity=‘New York’​(WAREHOUSE)).

    What the grader checks
    • (e) is the classic “all” query: ÷\div÷ (or the double difference) is expected. σCity=‘New York’\sigma_{\text{City=`New York'}}σCity=‘New York’​ followed by a join returns orders shipped from some NY warehouse, an existential answer worth 0 for the “all” criterion. The dividend must be projected to (Order#, Warehouse#) first.
    • (c) groups on Cust#; grouping on Cname merges namesakes.
    • (b) CUSTOMER∗\mathbin{*}∗WAREHOUSE, if it appears, joins on City, which is a wrong condition.

    Verified with the Python RA evaluator on a test instance: two customers named Jose Lopez; an order shipped from both NY warehouses, one from only one, one from Boston and NY; a late part shipment; and the empty-NY\mathit{NY}NY case, which returned every shipped order as A4 says.

    8.20Sales-trip queries (schema of Exercise 5.15)E&N Ex. 8.20 · p. 283

    Specify the following queries in relational algebra on the database schema given in Exercise 5.15: SALESPERSON(Ssn, Name, Start_year, Dept_no); TRIP(Ssn, From_city, To_city, Departure_date, Return_date, Trip_id); EXPENSE(Trip_id, Account#, Amount). (A trip can be charged to one or more accounts.)

    1. Give the details (all attributes of trip relation) for trips that exceeded $2,000 in expenses.
    2. Print the Ssns of salespeople who took trips to Honolulu.
    3. Print the total trip expenses incurred by the salesperson with SSN = ‘234-56-7890’.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. FKs: TRIP.Ssn → SALESPERSON.Ssn and EXPENSE.Trip_id → TRIP.Trip_id. Why: the answer to 5.15; Trip_id is the only attribute that TRIP and EXPENSE share.
    2. (a) A trip’s expenses are the sum over all the accounts it is charged to, and “exceeded” means >2000>2000>2000. Why: a trip can be charged to several accounts, so one EXPENSE tuple may be only a part of the trip’s cost.

    (a) Trips with total expenses above $2000

    TT←ρTT(Trip_id, Total)(Trip_id ISUM Amount(EXPENSE))BIG←πTrip_id(σTotal > 2000(TT))RESULT←BIG∗TRIP\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{TT} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{TT(Trip\_id, Total)}}\left({}_{\text{Trip\_id}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Amount}}\left(\textsf{EXPENSE}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{BIG} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Trip\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Total $>$ 2000}}\left(\mathit{TT}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \mathit{BIG} \mathbin{*} \textsf{TRIP}\end{array}TTBIGRESULT​←←←​ρTT(Trip_id, Total)​(Trip_id​ISUM Amount​(EXPENSE))πTrip_id​(σTotal > 2000​(TT))BIG∗TRIP​

    The joined result has exactly the attributes of TRIP, because BIG\mathit{BIG}BIG contributes only Trip_id. A trip charged $1500 to each of two accounts has a total of $3000 and qualifies, even though no single expense tuple exceeds $2000.

    (b) Salespeople who went to Honolulu

    RESULT←πSsn(σTo_city = ‘Honolulu’(TRIP))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn}}\left(\sigma_{\text{To\_city = `Honolulu'}}\left(\textsf{TRIP}\right)\right)\end{array}RESULT​←​πSsn​(σTo_city = ‘Honolulu’​(TRIP))​

    (c) Total expenses of salesperson 234-56-7890

    MYT←πTrip_id(σSsn = ‘234-56-7890’(TRIP))RESULT←ρRESULT(Total_expenses)( ISUM Amount(MYT∗EXPENSE))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{MYT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Trip\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Ssn = `234-56-7890'}}\left(\textsf{TRIP}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{RESULT(Total\_expenses)}}\left({}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Amount}}\left(\mathit{MYT} \mathbin{*} \textsf{EXPENSE}\right)\right)\end{array}MYTRESULT​←←​πTrip_id​(σSsn = ‘234-56-7890’​(TRIP))ρRESULT(Total_expenses)​(​ISUM Amount​(MYT∗EXPENSE))​

    The SUM runs over the full EXPENSE tuples, keyed by (Trip_id, Account#), so equal amounts are not merged.

    Answer

    (a) TRIP∗πTrip_id(σTotal>2000(Trip_id ISUM Amount(EXPENSE)))\textsf{TRIP} \mathbin{*} \pi_{\text{Trip\_id}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Total$>$2000}}\left({}_{\text{Trip\_id}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Amount}}\left(\textsf{EXPENSE}\right)\right)\right)TRIP∗πTrip_id​(σTotal>2000​(Trip_id​ISUM Amount​(EXPENSE))) (with the rename); (b) πSsn(σTo_city=‘Honolulu’(TRIP))\pi_{\text{Ssn}}\left(\sigma_{\text{To\_city=`Honolulu'}}\left(\textsf{TRIP}\right)\right)πSsn​(σTo_city=‘Honolulu’​(TRIP)); (c)  ISUM Amount(⋯ ){}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Amount}}\left(\cdots\right)​ISUM Amount​(⋯) over that salesperson’s expense tuples.

    What the grader checks
    • (a) σAmount>2000(EXPENSE)\sigma_{\text{Amount$>$2000}}\left(\textsf{EXPENSE}\right)σAmount>2000​(EXPENSE) tests single charges, not trip totals. State the reading if you use it; otherwise it does not match the question.
    • (c)  ISUM Amount(πAmount(⋯ )){}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{SUM Amount}}\left(\pi_{\text{Amount}}\left(\cdots\right)\right)​ISUM Amount​(πAmount​(⋯)) is wrong. In the test instance three $1500 charges collapsed to one and gave $1500 instead of $4500.

    Verified on a test instance (one trip split $1500+$1500, one single charge of $2500, one of exactly $2000) with the Python RA evaluator.

    8.21Enrolment/textbook queries (schema of Exercise 5.16)E&N Ex. 8.21 · p. 284

    Specify the following queries in relational algebra on the database schema given in Exercise 5.16: STUDENT(Ssn, Name, Major, Bdate); COURSE(Course#, Cname, Dept); ENROLL(Ssn, Course#, Quarter, Grade); BOOK_ADOPTION(Course#, Quarter, Book_isbn); TEXT(Book_isbn, Book_title, Publisher, Author).

    1. List the number of courses taken by all students named John Smith in Winter 2009 (i.e., Quarter=W09).
    2. Produce a list of textbooks (include Course#, Book_isbn, Book_title) for courses offered by the ‘CS’ department that have used more than two books.
    3. List any department that has all its adopted books published by ‘Pearson Publishing’.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. FKs: ENROLL.Ssn → STUDENT, ENROLL.Course# and BOOK_ADOPTION.Course# → COURSE, BOOK_ADOPTION.Book_isbn → TEXT. Why: the answer to 5.16. The printed key of BOOK_ADOPTION is (Course#, Quarter) (one book per course per quarter); the solution below does not rely on that.
    2. (a) There may be several students named John Smith. The answer gives one count per John Smith (grouped by Ssn). Why: “list the number … taken by all students named John Smith” asks for a list; the single total over all of them is  ICOUNT Course#(⋯ ){}_{\text{}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Course\#}}\left(\cdots\right)​ICOUNT Course#​(⋯) and is accepted if stated.
    3. (b) “Used more than two books” means more than two distinct Book_isbn values over all quarters. Why: the same book adopted in two quarters is still one book.
    4. (c) “Its adopted books” are the books adopted by any course of the department. A department whose courses adopted no books satisfies “all” vacuously and is listed. Why: a universal condition over an empty set is true (as in the RA-I key). The alternative reading, that a department must have adopted at least one book, is shown too.
    5. Publisher is never NULL. Why: with NULLs, ≠\neq= would be unknown and the difference would wrongly keep the department.

    (a) Courses taken in W09 by each John Smith

    JS←πSsn(σName = ‘John Smith’(STUDENT))W09←σQuarter = ‘W09’(ENROLL)RESULT←ρRESULT(Ssn, Num_courses)(Ssn ICOUNT Course#(JS∗W09))\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{JS} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Ssn}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Name = `John Smith'}}\left(\textsf{STUDENT}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{W09} &\leftarrow& \sigma_{\text{Quarter = `W09'}}\left(\textsf{ENROLL}\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{RESULT(Ssn, Num\_courses)}}\left({}_{\text{Ssn}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Course\#}}\left(\mathit{JS} \mathbin{*} \mathit{W09}\right)\right)\end{array}JSW09RESULT​←←←​πSsn​(σName = ‘John Smith’​(STUDENT))σQuarter = ‘W09’​(ENROLL)ρRESULT(Ssn, Num_courses)​(Ssn​ICOUNT Course#​(JS∗W09))​

    JS\mathit{JS}JS keeps only Ssn, so the natural join is on Ssn alone. Within one quarter an ENROLL tuple is one course, so COUNT counts courses.

    (b) Textbooks of CS courses that used more than two books

    CSC←πCourse#(σDept = ‘CS’(COURSE))CB←πCourse#, Book_isbn(BOOK_ADOPTION∗CSC)NB←ρNB(Course#, Nbooks)(Course# ICOUNT Book_isbn(CB))MANY←πCourse#(σNbooks > 2(NB))RESULT←πCourse#, Book_isbn, Book_title((CB∗MANY)∗TEXT)\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{CSC} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Course\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Dept = `CS'}}\left(\textsf{COURSE}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{CB} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Course\#, Book\_isbn}}\left(\textsf{BOOK\_ADOPTION} \mathbin{*} \mathit{CSC}\right) \\ \mathit{NB} &\leftarrow& \rho_{\text{NB(Course\#, Nbooks)}}\left({}_{\text{Course\#}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Book\_isbn}}\left(\mathit{CB}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{MANY} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Course\#}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Nbooks $>$ 2}}\left(\mathit{NB}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Course\#, Book\_isbn, Book\_title}}\left((\mathit{CB} \mathbin{*} \mathit{MANY}) \mathbin{*} \textsf{TEXT}\right)\end{array}CSCCBNBMANYRESULT​←←←←←​πCourse#​(σDept = ‘CS’​(COURSE))πCourse#, Book_isbn​(BOOK_ADOPTION∗CSC)ρNB(Course#, Nbooks)​(Course#​ICOUNT Book_isbn​(CB))πCourse#​(σNbooks > 2​(NB))πCourse#, Book_isbn, Book_title​((CB∗MANY)∗TEXT)​

    CB\mathit{CB}CB is a set of (course, book) pairs, so the projection removes repeated adoptions of a book (A3). The projection is deliberate here: COUNT then counts distinct books. MANY\mathit{MANY}MANY is the qualifying courses, and the last step lists their books with titles.

    (c) Departments all of whose adopted books are by Pearson Publishing

    DP←πDept, Publisher((COURSE∗BOOK_ADOPTION)∗TEXT)BAD←πDept(σPublisher ≠ ‘Pearson Publishing’(DP))RESULT←πDept(COURSE)−BAD\begin{array}{rcl}\mathit{DP} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dept, Publisher}}\left((\textsf{COURSE} \mathbin{*} \textsf{BOOK\_ADOPTION}) \mathbin{*} \textsf{TEXT}\right) \\ \mathit{BAD} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Publisher $\neq$ `Pearson Publishing'}}\left(\mathit{DP}\right)\right) \\ \mathit{RESULT} &\leftarrow& \pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\textsf{COURSE}\right) - \mathit{BAD}\end{array}DPBADRESULT​←←←​πDept, Publisher​((COURSE∗BOOK_ADOPTION)∗TEXT)πDept​(σPublisher = ‘Pearson Publishing’​(DP))πDept​(COURSE)−BAD​

    DP\mathit{DP}DP gives the publishers of the books each department adopted. BAD\mathit{BAD}BAD is the departments with at least one non-Pearson book. The difference leaves the departments with none, including (A4) departments that adopted no book. Alternative (stated reading: at least one adoption): RESULT←πDept(DP)−BAD\mathit{RESULT}\leftarrow \pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\mathit{DP}\right) - \mathit{BAD}RESULT←πDept​(DP)−BAD.

    Answer

    (a) Ssn ICOUNT Course#(JS∗σQuarter=‘W09’(ENROLL)){}_{\text{Ssn}}\,\mathfrak{I}_{\text{COUNT Course\#}}\left(\mathit{JS}\mathbin{*}\sigma_{\text{Quarter=`W09'}}\left(\textsf{ENROLL}\right)\right)Ssn​ICOUNT Course#​(JS∗σQuarter=‘W09’​(ENROLL)); (b) count distinct books per CS course, keep >2>2>2, list (Course#, Book_isbn, Book_title); (c) πDept(COURSE)−πDept(σPublisher≠‘Pearson Publishing’(⋯ ))\pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\textsf{COURSE}\right) - \pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Publisher$\neq$`Pearson Publishing'}}\left(\cdots\right)\right)πDept​(COURSE)−πDept​(σPublisher=‘Pearson Publishing’​(⋯)).

    What the grader checks
    • (c) is an “all” query. πDept(σPublisher=‘Pearson Publishing’(DP))\pi_{\text{Dept}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Publisher=`Pearson Publishing'}}\left(\mathit{DP}\right)\right)πDept​(σPublisher=‘Pearson Publishing’​(DP)) is existential (it lists departments with some Pearson book) and loses the “all” marks. Use difference (or ÷\div÷). State what happens to departments with no adoptions.
    • (b) Without the projection to (Course#, Book_isbn), COUNT counts adoptions. In the test instance a course that used one book in two quarters plus a second book was wrongly counted as 3 and wrongly included.
    • (a) Group on Ssn, not on Name (namesakes), or state that one total is wanted.

    Verified on a test instance (two John Smiths; a CS course with 3 distinct books and one with a repeated book; departments with all-Pearson, mixed and no adoptions) with the Python RA evaluator.

Reading (c) as left and (d) as right is the standard solution. Under the other reading, the grader box gives the left outer join on Q=B.

    What the grader checks
    • A theta join keeps both join columns (P and A). Only a natural join drops the duplicate.
    • In an outer join, check that every tuple of the preserved side appears at least once. A matched tuple appears once per match, not once in total: in (c), (10,a,5) appears twice.

    16  Exam cheat sheet

    Basics

    • Closed algebra: every operator returns a relation, so expressions nest. RA is procedural; calculus is declarative; same power (basic RA = safe TRC/DRC).
    • Set semantics: results are sets; π\piπ and ∪\cup∪ remove duplicates. Inside an aggregate, duplicate values are kept.

    Unary operators (8.1)

    • SELECT σc(R)\sigma_c(R)σc​(R): tuples satisfying ccc (and/or/not of A θ cA\,\theta\,cAθc, A θ BA\,\theta\,BAθB). One tuple at a time: never compares two tuples (needs a join). Degree =deg⁡R=\deg R=degR; 0≤∣⋅∣≤∣R∣0\le|\cdot|\le|R|0≤∣⋅∣≤∣R∣. NULL comparison is UNKNOWN: not selected.
    • σ\sigmaσ rules: commutative; cascade σc1(σc2(R))=σc1∧c2(R)\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R))=\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2}(R)σc1​​(σc2​​(R))=σc1​∧c2​​(R). Selectivity =∣σc(R)∣/∣R∣=|\sigma_c(R)|/|R|=∣σc​(R)∣/∣R∣.

    • Leaves = relations, internal nodes = operators, root = result; fixes an execution order (optimizer input).

    • Valid: push σ\sigmaσ to the side whose attrs it uses; σc1∧c2(R⋈S)=σc1(R)⋈σc2(S)\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2}(R\bowtie S)=\sigma_{c_1}(R)\bowtie\sigma_{c_2}(S)σc1​∧c2​​(R⋈S)=σc1​​(R)⋈σc2​​(S). For ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕ push only onto the preserved side.

    Query-writing patterns

    • Method: assumptions with reasons →\to→ relations →\to→ FK–PK join paths →\to→ selections early →\to→ project at end →\to→ name every step (T←…T\leftarrow\dotsT←…).
    • For all: πkey,item(actual)÷required\pi_{\text{key,item}}(\text{actual})\div\text{required}πkey,item​(actual)÷required, or C−πkey((C×required)−actual)C-\pi_{\text{key}}((C\times\text{required})-\text{actual})C−πkey​((C×required)−actual).
    • None / no: πkey(all)−πkey(those with)\pi_{\text{key}}(\text{all})-\pi_{\text{key}}(\text{those with})πkey​(all)−πkey​(those with).
    • At least two: ρ(E1,P1)(W)×ρ(E2,P2)(W)\rho_{(E1,P1)}(W)\times\rho_{(E2,P2)}(W)ρ(E1,P1)​(W)×ρ(E2,P2)​(W), then σE1=E2∧P1≠P2\sigma_{E1=E2\wedge P1\neq P2}σE1=E2∧P1=P2​, πE1\pi_{E1}πE1​; or I\mathfrak{I}I COUNT then σ≥2\sigma_{\ge2}σ≥2​.
    • Max without I\mathfrak{I}I: πkey(R)−πR1.key(σR1.v<R2.v(R1×R2))\pi_{\text{key}}(R)-\pi_{R_1.\text{key}}(\sigma_{R_1.v<R_2.v}(R_1\times R_2))πkey​(R)−πR1​.key​(σR1​.v<R2​.v​(R1​×R2​)).
    • Counts incl. zero: ⟕\mathbin{\text{⟕}}⟕ to the groups, COUNT a right-side attr (NULLs ignored).
    • Some vs all: “works on some dept-5 project” = join; “all” = ÷\div÷.

    Traps that cost marks

    • Natural join with no common name (EMPLOYEE ∗\mathbin{*}∗ WORKS_ON) = product: 0 for that criterion; ×\times× with no σ\sigmaσ, same.
    • Natural join equating unintended attrs (branch Address = borrower Address; CUSTOMER ∗\mathbin{*}∗ WAREHOUSE on City).
    • Existential answer for “all” (σ\sigmaσ + join, >>>MIN instead of >>>MAX, σv1>v2\sigma_{v_1>v_2}σv1​>v2​​ alone): 0. “No/none” via σ≠\sigma_{\neq}σ=​ instead of −-−: 0.
    • Undefined expressions (non-compatible ∪/−\cup/-∪/−, ambiguous or missing attribute): 0.
    • π\piπ before SUM/AVG/COUNT collapses equal values (45 not 55; 34000 avg). Keep the key.
    • Grouping on a name not a key (namesakes merge); counting after a join that multiplies rows.
    • Self-join copies not renamed; correlated conditions split across sub-expressions.
    • Theta join keeps both join columns. Outer join: NULLs on the non-preserved side; matched tuple once per match.
    • “More than five” is >5>5>5; “before/younger” strict. Two answers unmarked: the weaker is graded.

    Exam moves

    • State one assumption with a reason per part (about 1 of 5 marks): keys, NULLs, ties, empty divisor.
    • Spot the quantifier first: some = join, all = ÷\div÷, none = −-−, max = self-join difference.
    • Equivalent expressions get full marks; any standard notation (γ\gammaγ or I\mathfrak{I}I) is fine.
